explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that chronic recurrent wheals that do not resolve with antihistamines, along with fever, arthralgia, elevated CRP level, and neutrophilic infiltrate on skin biopsy are characteristic of Schnitzler syndrome. A test for Lyme disease (choice A) is not recommended because diffuse wheals are not characteristic of Lyme disease. Antibiotics (choice C) are not indicated because the patient’s symptoms were not consistent with a skin infection. There was no evidence of vasculitis on skin biopsy, so treatment with methotrexate (choice D) is not indicated. Schnitzler syndrome is a rare systemic autoinflammatory disease of unknown etiology, with approximately 350 case reports published worldwide.1-3Wheals are typically the presenting symptom of Schnitzler syndrome.1,2Other common symptoms are fever (72%), joint pain (68%), and bone pain (55%).1Schnitzler syndrome is estimated to affect less than 1% of individuals with chronic urticaria and up to 1.5% of patients with monoclonal IgM gammopathy.4The median age of onset is 51 years, with a male to female ratio of 1.5.1 Schnitzler syndrome is diagnosed based on presence of 2 major criteria: chronic urticarial rash (wheals) and a monoclonal IgM (85%) or IgG (7%) gammopathy, although isolated IgA monoclonal gammopathy has been recently described.1,2,5In addition, the diagnosis requires presence of least 2 minor criteria (with IgM monoclonal gammopathy) or 3 minor criteria (with IgG monoclonal gammopathy), including recurrent unexplained fever, leukocytosis, and/or elevated CRP level, a neutrophilic dermal infiltrate on skin biopsy, or findings of abnormal bone remodeling (based on bone scintigraphy, magnetic resonance imaging, or elevated bone alkaline phosphatase level on blood testing).6 Schnitzler syndrome is likely underdiagnosed, and there is an average diagnostic delay of 3.3 years after onset of symptoms.2The differential diagnosis of Schnitzler syndrome includes chronic spontaneous urticaria,7urticarial vasculitis, cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome, adult-onset Still disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus. Antihistamines, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, colchicine, and oral glucocorticoids typically have limited efficacy for patients with Schnitzler syndrome and may be associated with long-term adverse effects. However, treatment with IL-1/IL-1 receptor antagonists (anakinra, rilonacept, and canakinumab) is effective, although none of these treatments are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for Schnitzler syndrome.1,2,8,9A systematic review of 7 studies (34 patients) reported that canakinumab treatment was associated with a complete response in 58.6% and a partial response in all remaining patients over a cumulative follow-up of 253 months.9The most common adverse event was infection (n = 79).9A 4-year follow-up study of 17 patients with Schnitzler syndrome reported long-term benefits of canakinumab, with most patients having no, minimal, or mild residual symptoms.8 Patients with Schnitzler syndrome, similar to those with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance,10are at increased risk of hematologic malignancies. In a study of 281 patients with Schnitzler syndrome, over a median follow-up of 8 years, 12% developed a hematologic malignancy; of these malignancies, 60% were Waldenström macroglobulinemia.1 A monoclonal gammopathy of the IgA type lambda was detected in a serum immunofixation test. Findings on bone marrow biopsy were normal. Results of hepatitis B and C antibody testing, interferon-gamma release assay, and HIV serology were negative. Treatment with anakinra (100 mg subcutaneously daily) resulted in resolution of the fever and wheals, but the patient’s arthralgia, myalgia, and fatigue persisted. After 9 months, anakinra was stopped and canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks) was started. At her most recent visit, 46 months after presentation, the patient had no wheals, fever, or myalgia and only mild intermittent arthralgia in her right shoulder while taking canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks). Results of complete blood cell count with differential, serum immunofixation test, and free light chain ratio have remained unchanged and will continue to be checked every 6 months to screen for lymphoproliferative disorders.

caption: Color fundus photography at patient presentation suggesting mild bilateral disc edema (greater in the left eye than in the right) evidenced by superonasal disc margin blurring and elevation (brackets) and vessel obscuration.
scenario: A 30-year-old nulliparous woman with migraines, depression, and obesity (12.7-kg [28-lb] weight gain over the prior 2 years) presented to the primary care clinic with 1 month of daily headaches, transient bilateral blurry vision, and persistent vision loss in the temporal region of the right eye. She experienced right-sided temporal and frontal headaches accompanied by intermittent auditory hissing, without auras. The headaches lasted for several hours each day, worsened when she was lying flat, and were temporarily relieved by acetaminophen. She took no daily medications or supplements but had a contraceptive etonogestrel implant that had been placed 9 months prior to presentation. Her temperature was 37.1 °C (98.8 °F); heart rate, 95/min; blood pressure, 106/70 mm Hg; height, 1.57 m (5 ft 2 in); weight, 113.9 kg (251 lb); and body mass index, 45 (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in meters). Her pupillary reflexes were brisk bilaterally, without a relative afferent pupillary defect. By visual field testing to confrontation, she had a temporal visual field defect in the right eye. Her physical examination findings were otherwise normal. The patient was referred for same-day ophthalmology evaluation, which revealed visual acuity of 20/20 bilaterally and normal extraocular movements without nystagmus or ocular misalignment. Mild bilateral papilledema was seen on dilated fundoscopy (Figure). Automated visual field testing demonstrated enlargement of the physiologic (temporal) blind spot in the right eye and mild constriction of the left nasal visual field.

options.A: Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging and magnetic resonance venography
options.B: Perform a lumbar puncture in the lateral decubitus position
options.C: Prescribe prednisone (40 mg by mouth daily for 7 days)

answer: Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetic resonance venography (MRV)
distractors: Perform a lumbar puncture in the lateral decubitus position
Prescribe prednisone (40 mg by mouth daily for 7 days)
Remove the birth control implant
explanation: A. Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetic resonance venography (MRV) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that symptoms of positional headache, visual blurring, and pulsatile tinnitus are characteristic of IIH in a female with obesity. Lumbar puncture (choice B) should not be performed until neuroimaging has confirmed absence of an intracranial lesion causing papilledema. Prednisone (choice C) is incorrect because the patient’s symptoms were not characteristic of optic neuritis or temporal arteritis. Removal of the birth control implant (choice D) is not recommended because there is no known association between hormonal contraception and IIH.1 IIH is a condition of elevated intracranial pressure without a known cause. It is diagnosed using the modified Dandy criteria, which include (1) symptoms of elevated intracranial pressure such as headache, tinnitus, diplopia, and/or visual disturbances without secondary etiologies (eg, intracranial tumors, venous sinus thrombosis, infection, or medications such as vitamin A derivatives, tetracyclines, lithium, and human growth hormone); (2) papilledema on fundus examination; and (3) elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure on lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position (opening pressure >25 cm H2O in adults; >28 cm H2O in children). IIH primarily affects women of childbearing age and is strongly associated with obesity.2A cross-sectional study of 85 million US patients reported that the prevalence of IIH increased from 7.3 individuals per 100 000 in 2015 to 9.9 per 100 000 in 2022,3correlating with increasing US obesity rates. The pathogenesis of IIH is unclear but may involve hypersecretion and/or decreased absorption of cerebrospinal fluid related to increased levels of androgens, glucocorticoids, glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), and inflammatory cytokines associated with central adiposity.4 First-line treatment for IIH is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (eg, acetazolamide), which causes a rapid reduction of intracranial pressure through decreased cerebrospinal fluid production. Patients with suspected IIH may be treated with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor before confirmation of papilledema, if ophthalmologic examination cannot be not performed expeditiously. If brain MRI/MRV shows no intracranial lesions, patients with suspected IIH should undergo a diagnostic lumbar puncture to determine if cerebrospinal fluid pressure is elevated. While lumbar puncture temporarily decreases intracranial pressure by removing cerebrospinal fluid and may relieve IIH symptoms in the short term, it is not definitive therapy. The combination of a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and weight loss (5%-10%) is effective at improving peripheral vision, papilledema, and vision-related quality-of-life measures.5Small randomized trials of bariatric surgery and a GLP-1 receptor agonist (exenatide) in patients with IIH have demonstrated decreased intracranial pressure compared with control patients.6,7Patients with IIH and fulminant vision loss, or those whose symptoms do not improve or worsen despite medical therapy, may require emergent ventriculoperitoneal shunting, optic nerve sheath fenestration, or venous sinus stenting, although evidence for efficacy of surgical options is lacking.8 The visual prognosis of patients with IIH depends on papilledema grade and visual symptom severity at diagnosis.9,10Untreated IIH can lead to permanent vision loss within several weeks, so early symptom recognition and treatment are important to avoid blindness. Serial ophthalmologic evaluation every 1 to 3 months with quantitative optical coherence tomography and automated visual field testing is indicated for all patients with IIH who have papilledema to evaluate response to therapy and guide treatment. Brain MRI/MRV performed on the day of presentation revealed no intracranial abnormalities but demonstrated diminutive transverse venous sinuses and prominent optic nerve sheath fluid bilaterally, suggestive of elevated intracranial pressure. Same-day lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position revealed a cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure of 33 cm H2O (reference, ≤25 cm H2O); examination of the cerebrospinal fluid showed normal levels of glucose and total protein and no pleocytosis. The patient was prescribed acetazolamide (500 mg 3 times daily) and was encouraged to exercise and make dietary modifications. At 1-month follow-up, she reported near-complete resolution of visual blurring and headaches and had lost 2.27 kg (5 lb). Ophthalmologic examination revealed no residual disc edema or visual field defects. She was advised to continue acetazolamide (500 mg 3 times daily) and to continue weight loss efforts.

scenario: A previously healthy 9-year-old boy presented to a primary care clinic with a 10-day history of a nonproductive cough without fever, wheeze, chest pain, or abdominal pain. His white blood cell count and C-reactive protein level were normal. A chest radiograph revealed an opacity in the lower right lobe. The patient underwent noncontrast computed tomography (CT) of the chest, which revealed a right anterior mediastinal mass. He was referred the same day to the surgery clinic, where his blood pressure was 113/81 mm Hg; heart rate, 98/min; respiratory rate, 20/min; and oxygen saturation, 98% while breathing room air. On physical examination, his chest wall appeared normal. Lung examination revealed diminished breath sounds in the right lower lung field. Levels of α-fetoprotein, human chorionic gonadotropin, and neuron-specific enolase were normal. A contrast-enhanced chest CT scan revealed a 10.4 × 7.8 × 7.8–cm mass in the right anterior mediastinum with a radiodensity of −121 Hounsfield units, consistent with fat (Figure).

options.A: Arrange for upper gastrointestinal tract endoscopy
options.B: Perform a percutaneous biopsy of the mass
options.C: Prescribe intravenous cefuroxime (20 mg/kg/d for 7 days)

answer: Schedule laparoscopic surgery
distractors: Arrange for upper gastrointestinal tract endoscopy
Perform a percutaneous biopsy of the mass
Prescribe intravenous cefuroxime (20 mg/kg/d for 7 days)
explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that presence of a fat-density mass in the thoracic cavity along with signs of a discontinuous diaphragm are characteristic of a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). Upper gastrointestinal tract endoscopy (choice A) is incorrect because the anterior mediastinal mass did not appear related to the esophagus or stomach. Percutaneous biopsy (choice B) is not recommended because it could penetrate herniated bowel and cause bleeding if the gastro-omental blood vessels are punctured. Prescribing antibiotics (choice C) is not indicated because the patient had no clinical signs of infection. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia is a developmental defect of the diaphragm, with an incidence rate of approximately 2.3 per 10 000 live births.1Mortality estimates range from 10% to 90%, based on factors such as the severity of the diaphragmatic defect, presence of other congenital malformations, and access to specialized care.1 The 3 types of CDH are Bochdalek hernias, hiatal hernias, and Morgagni hernias. Bochdalek hernias account for 95% of CDHs and are caused by absence of an intact posterolateral diaphragm; most (85%) occur on the left side.2Hiatal hernias are caused by developmental abnormality of the esophageal hiatus and lead to herniation of the gastroesophageal junction, stomach, or intestine through the esophageal hiatus. Morgagni hernias, which account for 2% to 4% of CDHs, are caused by congenital anteromedial subcostosternal defects.3 Two-thirds of all CDHs can be detected on routine fetal ultrasound; the mean gestational age at diagnosis is 22 to 24 weeks,1,2Infants with CDH often present with respiratory distress after birth, and most of these infants have a Bochdalek hernia. Among the 5% to 25% of children with CDH who have minimal or no symptoms in the neonatal period, CDH may be detected in childhood or even in adulthood. The incidence of CDH in adults is uncertain.4Once a CDH is identified, surgical repair is indicated to prevent complications, including bowel obstruction or incarceration. Due to the typically small size of the subcostosternal defect and location, Morgagni hernias are rarely identified on fetal ultrasound.5Between 34% and 50% of Morgagni hernias are associated with other congenital anomalies such as Down syndrome or atrioventricular septal defect.6,7Approximately two-thirds of patients with Morgagni hernia are symptomatic in infancy or childhood and present with respiratory symptoms such as recurrent chest infections or chronic cough (56%), gastrointestinal symptoms such as gastric pain and/or nausea and vomiting (19%), or a combination of pulmonary and gastrointestinal symptoms (6.8%).7-9Morgagni hernia may be identified in adulthood, presenting with respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms related to the hernia, or discovered incidentally on an imaging study during workup of an unrelated problem.7-9Patients with Morgagni hernia may rarely present with intestinal obstruction or respiratory distress requiring emergency surgery. On chest radiography, Morgagni hernias typically present as a radiolucent retrosternal paracardiac opacity, and, if the bowel is herniated into the chest, a retrosternal air-filled, tubelike opacity may be seen. When a solid organ such as the liver herniates through the diaphragmatic defect, the differential diagnosis includes atelectasis, pericardial fat pad, or intrathoracic tumors such as lipoblastoma and cardiac tumor. If Morgagni hernia is suspected based on chest radiography, an abdominal CT with intravenous contrast should be obtained to confirm the diagnosis. Once identified, repair of Morgagni hernia should be performed promptly, due to risk of bowel strangulation leading to bowel ischemia or perforation. Minimally invasive surgical techniques, including laparoscopic and thoracoscopic surgery, are the preferred approaches for CDH repair.8The placement of a patch or mesh may be considered if the defect is large or under significant tension.8,10 The patient underwent laparoscopic surgery, which revealed that a portion of the greater omentum had entered the right thoracic cavity through a retrosternal hernial defect. The defect was closed with 3 stitches using a U-shaped suture. At discharge from the hospital 6 days after surgery, the patient’s cough had resolved. Three months later, a noncontrast abdominal CT scan revealed a continuous diaphragm with no evidence of hernia recurrence; minimal fatty tissue, which likely represented the hernia sac; and a small effusion in the right cardiophrenic angle. At most recent follow-up 6 months after surgery, the patient was asymptomatic and had returned to his usual activities.

scenario: A 45-year-old man without significant medical history was evaluated for multiple asymptomatic skin lesions on non–sun-exposed areas of the body, which first appeared in the bilateral axillae 8 years prior to presentation. On physical examination, he had multiple erythematous macules and patches on the trunk; hyperpigmented patches on the intergluteal cleft and subgluteal fold; and atrophic, mottled, hypopigmented and hyperpigmented skin with telangiectasias (poikiloderma) in the axillae (Figure). There were no palpable lymph nodes. Laboratory analysis revealed a normal complete blood cell count, normal liver function test results, and normal levels of lactate dehydrogenase, creatinine, and fasting plasma glucose. Results of antinuclear antibody testing were negative.

options.A: Arrange for T-cell receptor (TCR) gene rearrangement testing
options.B: Check for anti-Scl-70 and anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies
options.D: Perform a skin biopsy with immunophenotyping of lymphocyte markers

answer: Perform a skin biopsy with immunophenotyping of lymphocyte markers
distractors: Arrange for T-cell receptor (TCR) gene rearrangement testing
Check for anti-Scl-70 and anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies
Measure glycated hemoglobin level
explanation: D. Perform a skin biopsy with immunophenotyping of lymphocyte markers The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that persistent hyperpigmented patches and poikiloderma located on non–sun-exposed body areas are characteristic of mycosis fungoides, which is diagnosed with a skin biopsy. TCR gene rearrangement testing (choice A) is performed only when mycosis fungoides is suspected and initial skin biopsy is inconclusive. Checking for anti-Scl-70 and anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies (choice B) is not recommended because the patient’s skin findings are not characteristic of systemic sclerosis. Screening for diabetes (choice C) is not indicated because the lesions are not consistent with acanthosis nigricans. Mycosis fungoides is the most common primary cutaneous lymphoma, constituting nearly 50% of all cases.1The incidence in Europe and the US is estimated at 5.42 per million per year, and the incidence has increased annually by 1.34% over the past 2 decades.2The median age of diagnosis is 55 to 60 years, with a male to female ratio of 2:1.3 The World Health Organization and the European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer classify mycosis fungoides into classic mycosis fungoides (88.6% of cases) and 3 variants.4Classic mycosis fungoides is a slowly progressive disease that occurs primarily on non–sun-exposed areas of skin and appears first as cutaneous patches, then cutaneous plaques, and later as exophytic or ulcerated tumors.3,4Findings of poikiloderma are suggestive of early mycosis fungoides, and pruritus is present in 80% of patients with mycosis fungoides.4Extracutaneous mycosis fungoides may occur rarely and can involve the lymph nodes, spleen, liver, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract. The pathogenesis of mycosis fungoides is not fully understood but involves clonal proliferation and malignant transformation of skin-homing CD4+memory T cells. No clear evidence supports any infectious, pharmacological, environmental, or occupational exposures as risk factors or causes of mycosis fungoides.3 The differential diagnosis of mycosis fungoides includes eczema, psoriasis, drug reactions, contact dermatitis, and other cutaneous B-cell and T-cell lymphomas. Diagnosis of mycosis fungoides is made with skin biopsy of patches or plaques, which typically reveals a bandlike lymphoid infiltrate in the superficial dermis, with atypical lymphocytes extending into the epidermis (epidermotropism). In tumor lesions, the neoplastic lymphoid infiltrate extends into the dermis. In 80% of cases, a CD4+/CD8–immunophenotype predominates in the lymphoid infiltrate.5The diagnosis is further supported by absence of antigens characteristic of normal T cells such as CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7. Staging of mycosis fungoides is based on evaluation of the skin (T), lymph nodes (N), metastases (M), and blood (B) and requires estimation of skin involvement; evaluation of lymph nodes (with biopsy of lymph nodes that are larger than 1.5 cm, firm, or fixed); assessment for other organ involvement with physical examination and basic laboratory assessment; and testing peripheral blood for atypical lymphocytes with cerebriform nuclei (Sézary cells).4,6Individuals with extensive cutaneous mycosis fungoides findings or possible extracutaneous involvement should undergo computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis or a positron emission tomography (PET)–CT scan to accurately stage mycosis fungoides. First-line therapy for early-stage mycosis fungoides, defined as stages IA to IIA, includes topical steroids and phototherapy, administered either as narrowband UV-B or psoralen plus UV-A (PUVA), which penetrates deeper into the dermis. Advanced-stage mycosis fungoides, defined as stages IIB to IV, requires systemic treatment and may include retinoids, interferon alfa, chemotherapy, targeted immunotherapy, and extracorporeal photochemotherapy6(extracorporeal exposure of white blood cells to the photosensitizing agent psoralen, followed by UV-A irradiation and reinfusion of the treated cells). Early-stage mycosis fungoides with limited skin and lymph node involvement (stages IA to IIA) has a 10-year survival rate of 70% to 90%. Patients with mycosis fungoides and tumor lesions are classified as having at least stage IIB disease, which is associated with a 10-year survival rate of 40%.7Patients with stage IVB (visceral involvement) disease have a median survival of 1.4 years and a disease-specific survival of 18% at 5 years.8 A left axillary skin biopsy demonstrated a bandlike lymphoid infiltrate in the superficial dermis and epidermotropism, both characteristic of mycosis fungoides. Immunohistochemical staining of the biopsy specimen revealed CD4+/CD8–T cells and absence of normal CD7 T-cell antigens. The patient was diagnosed with stage IB mycosis fungoides, based on a whole-body PET scan that showed no enlarged lymph nodes and absence of Sézary cells in the peripheral blood. He underwent PUVA therapy 2 to 3 times weekly for 15 months, and his skin lesions gradually resolved. Repeat left axillary skin biopsy performed 15 months after initial presentation showed minimal lymphocytic infiltrate without evidence of epidermotropism or atypia. The patient has continued PUVA once weekly, and at his most recent clinic visit, 52 months after initial presentation, he had no cutaneous manifestations of mycosis fungoides.

caption: A, Non–electrocardiogram-gated computed tomography scan of the chest obtained in the emergency department. Transthoracic echocardiography performed in the cardiology clinic demonstrated an ascending aortic aneurysm (B) and a bicuspid aortic valve (C).
scenario: A healthy 25-year-old woman was seen in the cardiology clinic 1 month after being diagnosed with an upper respiratory tract infection during an emergency department visit for 2 days of shortness of breath and low-grade fevers. A computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram performed in the emergency department revealed no pulmonary infiltrates, effusion, or embolism but identified an isolated 4.2-cm dilatation in the mid ascending aorta (Figure 1). In the cardiology clinic, her blood pressure was 118/85 mm/Hg and heart rate 65/min. A transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) demonstrated normal left and right ventricular function, a 4.3-cm ascending aortic aneurysm, and a bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) without evidence of aortic stenosis or regurgitation (Figure 1). Family history revealed that her father had a dissection of the ascending aorta repaired at age 60 years.

options.A: Arrange for urgent surgical aneurysm repair
options.B: Order an aortic electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated CT angiogram with contrast
options.C: Perform annual surveillance thoracic CT scans

answer: Order an aortic electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated CT angiogram with contrast.
distractors: Arrange for urgent surgical aneurysm repair
Perform annual surveillance thoracic CT scans
Prescribe metoprolol (25 mg twice daily)
explanation: Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (ATAA) and BAV B. Order an aortic electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated CT angiogram with contrast. The key to correct management is recognizing that an ascending aortic aneurysm detected on a standard imaging study should be evaluated with specialized CT imaging timed to diastole (ECG-gated;Figure 2) to reduce cardiac motion artifact. Choice A is incorrect because the patient did not meet indications for urgent surgical repair. Surveillance decisions (choice C) are appropriate only after fully evaluating the aneurysm. β-Blocker treatment (choice D) is not indicated with normal blood pressure. Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms involve dilation of the aortic root and/or ascending aorta extending into the proximal aortic arch and affect approximately 5.3 per 100 000 individuals per year worldwide.1Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm may expand asymptomatically and cause aortic rupture, which is associated with a mortality rate greater than 90%.1Incidence of ATAA is increased among individuals with BAV, which has a worldwide prevalence of 1% to 2%,2and among those with a family history of aortic dissection, familial connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome), or Turner syndrome.3Rarely, ATAAs are caused by syphilis or rheumatologic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or Takayasu disease.3Up to 56% of patients with BAV younger than age 30 years have a dilated ascending aorta (diameter 1.1 times greater than expected based on age, sex, and body surface area).2Patients with BAV have an approximately 9-fold increased relative risk for aortic dissection, although their absolute risk is low (0.68% lifetime).2,3A 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline recommended that first-degree relatives of patients with BAV, aortic root or ascending aorta aneurysms, or aortic dissection undergo aortic screening with a TTE, ECG-gated CT angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the thoracic aorta and that patients with familial BAV and/or thoracic aortic aneurysms should be referred for genetic testing.3 Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms are frequently diagnosed incidentally on a thoracic CT imaging study. Approximately 95% of patients with ATAA are asymptomatic at diagnosis, and 5% have nonspecific symptoms such as chest pain, back pain, dysphagia, or dyspnea.4Patients with ATAA should be evaluated for connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and family history of BAV, aortic aneurysm, and sudden death should be elicited. A TTE to evaluate left ventricular function, aortic valve, root, and the proximal ascending aorta, and an ECG-gated aortic CT angiogram with contrast, should be obtained. Thoracic aorta MRA is an alternative to CT and has similar sensitivity (100% vs 98%, respectively) and specificity (98% vs 98%, respectively) for aneurysm detection.5 For patients with ATAA, the 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline–recommended goal systolic blood pressure is less than 130/80 mm Hg.6The guideline recommends that patients with BAV who have an ascending aortic diameter 5.5 cm or greater undergo surgery to replace the aortic root and ascending aorta. Other surgical indications include ascending aortic cross-sectional area-height ratio 10 cm2/m or greater or aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater with risk factors for aortic dissection such as family history of aortic dissection, rapid aortic growth rate (>0.3 cm/y), or preconception in women with BAV and an aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater.6,7Patients with ATAA and BAV who do not meet indications for surgery should undergo annual echocardiography, CT, or MRA to assess for rapid aneurysm expansion (>0.3 cm/y) and progression of BAV.6 Surgical repair includes replacement of aneurysmal tissue with a polyester fiber conduit. For patients with ATAA and severe bicuspid aortic valve stenosis (aortic velocity >4 m/s, mean pressure gradient >40 mm Hg, aortic valve area <1.0 cm2) or aortic regurgitation, aortic valve replacement is typically recommended.6Surgery can often be performed through minimally invasive procedures, such as a hemisternotomy.8The 5-year survival rate after ascending aortic and root replacement is 89.9%.9After ATAA surgery, patients should receive surveillance imaging with CT or MRA within 1 year and, if stable, every 5 years thereafter to monitor for progression of aortic dilation.6 A ECG-gated CT angiogram demonstrated a 5.0-cm ATAA with a cross-sectional/height ratio of 11.7 cm2/m (Figure 2). Based on the patient’s aortic aneurysm size and family history of aortic dissection, she met criteria for surgery.3Ascending aortic replacement was performed minimally invasively, with 4 cm of ascending aorta excised and replaced with a polyester fiber conduit. She did not undergo aortic valve repair or replacement due to her young age and absence of aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation. She was discharged after a 4-day hospitalization. At a clinic visit 1 month later, the patient was asymptomatic and blood pressure was 110/80 mm Hg. Aortic surveillance will be performed with a ECG-gated CT scan 12 months postoperatively, and her first-degree relatives were offered screening for BAV and aortic aneurysm.

caption: Patient’s face at presentation, showing lighter skin pigmentation compared with her hands.
scenario: A previously healthy woman in her 40s presented with 6 months of bilateral leg edema, insomnia, and myalgias. One month after symptom onset, her creatinine level was 0.80 mg/dL (71 μmol/L) (reference, 0.50-1.19 mg/dL [44-105 μmol/L]) and 24-hour urine protein content was 8.7 g (reference <0.15 g). Kidney biopsy revealed thickening of the glomerular basement membrane with electron-dense deposits, consistent with membranous nephropathy, stage 2. She was treated with 3 days of methylprednisolone (500 mg) and cyclophosphamide (400 mg), followed by prednisolone (1 mg/kg/d) for 8 weeks, subsequently tapered by 10 mg every 4 weeks. Four weeks after initial treatment, proteinuria had decreased to less than 0.5 g/d, but proteinuria increased to 6.72 g/d when the prednisolone dosage was decreased to 20 mg/d. At current presentation, she had normal vital signs, pitting edema of the ankles bilaterally, mild resting tremor in both hands, and lighter pigmentation of her facial skin compared with other areas of her body (Figure). Laboratory testing revealed a serum creatinine level of 0.88 mg/dL (78 μmol/L) (reference, 0.59-1.28 mg/dL [52-113 μmol/L]); 24-hour urine protein content, 6.91 g (reference, <0.15 g); and serum albumin level, 28.4 g/L (reference, 40-55 g/L). She reported difficulty sleeping, myalgias, and paresthesias in her fingertips. She had no dyspnea, chest pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, arthralgias, or rash. The patient did not smoke cigarettes, use illicit drugs, or take herbal supplements but had used skin-lightening cream on her face daily for the prior 7 months. Findings of brain and spine magnetic resonance imaging scans, electroencephalography, and electromyography were unremarkable.

options.A: Arrange a quadriceps muscle biopsy
options.B: Check blood for heavy metals

answer: Check blood for heavy metals
distractors: Arrange a quadriceps muscle biopsy
Order serum protein electrophoresis
Repeat the kidney biopsy
explanation: Mercury toxicity associated with skin-lightening cream B. Check blood for heavy metals The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that proteinuria, insomnia, paresthesias, and myalgias are characteristic of mercury intoxication, which may occur with use of contaminated skin-lightening products. Because this patient did not have muscle weakness, a muscle biopsy (choice A) is not recommended. Serum protein electrophoresis (choice C) is not indicated because insomnia, paresthesias, and myalgias are not typical symptoms of multiple myeloma or amyloidosis. Membranous nephropathy was diagnosed on prior kidney biopsy, so a repeat kidney biopsy (choice D) is unnecessary. Mercury is a heavy metal that is present in the earth’s crust and exists in elemental, organic, and inorganic forms, all of which may be toxic to humans. Although the pathogenesis is not fully understood, conjugation of mercury to sulfhydryl groups of proteins throughout the body may inactivate enzymes and increase oxidative stress, inflammation, cytotoxicity, apoptosis, and autoimmunity.1The toxic manifestations of mercury depend on its form, dose, route (inhalation, ingestion, dermal absorption, or injection), and duration of exposure.2Exposure to inorganic mercury, which includes mercurous and mercuric salts, can occur in certain industries (eg, mining, chemical and metal processing), via ingestion of mercury-containing medications, or with use of skin-lightening products.3-5Mercury compounds are readily absorbed through intact skin and inhibit melanin production, resulting in lighter skin color.4,6Although the World Health Organization recommends that mercury levels in skin products should not exceed 1 ppm,5skin-lightening products containing mercury levels greater than 1000 ppm are available in the US and other areas of the world.3,6 Some individuals with chronic exposure to inorganic mercury salts are asymptomatic despite high blood levels of mercury.5Others develop symptoms primarily due to effects on the kidneys and central nervous system; such symptoms manifest months to years after initial mercury exposure.5Inorganic mercury deposition in the kidneys often causes nephrotic syndrome due to membranous nephropathy2or, less commonly, minimal change disease.6Common neuropsychiatric effects include headache, dizziness, insomnia, vision changes, depression, anxiety, tremors, paresthesias, and ataxia.5,7 The differential diagnosis of mercury poisoning includes systemic lupus erythematosus, nephrotic syndrome, polyneuropathy, pheochromocytoma, depression, and dementia.5The diagnosis of mercury intoxication is often delayed due to the nonspecific and heterogeneous nature of associated symptoms and lack of clinician awareness about the condition.2,5,8,9Inorganic mercury intoxication should be suspected in patients with nephrotic syndrome and neuropsychiatric symptoms who have a history of mercury exposure or use skin-lightening products. The diagnosis is made based on elevated levels of mercury in urine or whole blood.5 First-line treatment of mercury intoxication due to skin-lightening cream is discontinuation of the product.5Chelation therapy with dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) or D-penicillamine is indicated for symptomatic patients with abnormal urine or blood mercury levels.5Dimercapto-1-propanesulfonic acid may be used for patients who have adverse effects from DMSA.5Although symptoms of mercury intoxication often improve or resolve after chelation, the prognosis depends upon the severity of clinical presentation, concentration of mercury in the product, and duration of use.5 A heavy metal test revealed a blood mercury level of 16.7 μg/L (83.3 nmol/L) (reference, <2.5 μg/L [12.5 nmol/L]). A random urine mercury level was 22.2 μg/L (110.7 nmol/L) (reference, <2.5 μg/L [12.5 nmol/L]). Although mercury was not listed on the product label, the patient’s facial cream was found to contain 36 000 ppm of inorganic mercury. She discontinued this cream and underwent chelation therapy with intramuscular DMSA (250 mg daily) for 3 days. Three additional rounds of chelation with DMSA were administered over 3 days with a 4-day interval between rounds. Her neurologic symptoms of insomnia, myalgias, and paresthesias resolved after the second round of chelation, and after the fourth round, she had minimal proteinuria (0.5 g/d) and a normal blood mercury level (2.4 μg/L [12 nmol/L]). The patient was discharged home after a 31-day hospitalization. Twelve months after initial presentation, she was asymptomatic, and laboratory tests revealed normal creatinine, albumin, and urine protein levels.

caption: Accepted dual-stage diagnostic algorithms for syphilis testing according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
scenario: A 54-year-old woman was evaluated for a rash on her face, trunk, arms, and proximal thighs that developed 10 months prior to presentation. She had arthralgias and fatigue and reported transient oral ulcers on her buccal mucosa. The patient had false-positive syphilis test results during 2 pregnancies, 25 and 22 years prior, based on a positive blood rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test result (titer, 1:2 [reference, nonreactive]) and negative fluorescent treponemal antibody (FTA-ABS) test result. On current presentation, she had erythematous annular and indurated plaques on her face, trunk, and extremities (Supplement). Laboratory testing revealed positive cardiolipin IgM (150 U/mL [reference, <13 U/mL]) and cardiolipin IgG (40 U/mL [reference, <15 U/mL]) antibodies. RPR titer was 1:1024. Skin biopsy revealed a dense perivascular and periadnexal infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells. The patient was not taking any new prescriptions or over-the-counter medications and did not use herbal supplements. She had no history of sexually transmitted infections and was sexually active with 1 male partner for the past 12 months.

options.A: Primary syphilis is likely.
options.B: Secondary syphilis is likely.
options.C: The rapid plasma reagin is a false-positive result due to cardiolipin antibodies.
options.D: The rapid plasma reagin is a false-positive result from prior pregnancies.

answer: Secondary syphilis is likely.
distractors: Primary syphilis is likely.
The rapid plasma reagin is a false-positive result due to cardiolipin antibodies.
The rapid plasma reagin is a false-positive result from prior pregnancies.
explanation: B. Secondary syphilis is likely. Nontreponemal tests (NTTs) include RPR, VDRL, and toluidine red unheated serum test. NTTs assess serum reactivity to a lecithin-cholesterol-cardiolipin antigen to identify IgG and IgM antibodies produced by individuals infected withTreponema pallidum. NTT results are semiquantitative, such that the amount of IgM and IgG antibodies generally reflects the activity of syphilitic infection.1NTT titers are useful to monitor response to treatment. A 4-fold dilutional decrease indicates effective therapy, and NTTs may become nonreactive within 1 year after treatment initiation.2-5The sensitivity of NTTs for a diagnosis of syphilis is 95% to 100%6and specificity is 81% to 96%.5False-positive NTT results may occur in patients with lupus erythematosus, vasculitis, tuberculosis, viral pneumonia, malignancy, bacterial endocarditis, intravenous drug use, ulcerative colitis, hepatitis C, rickettsial disease, or pregnancy.7Low, false-positive RPR titer results (such as 1:2 or 1:4) occur in 2% to 5% of individuals without syphilis infection.3,6,8False-negative NTT results can occur during the first 3 weeks of primary syphilis infection or in patients with very high antibody titers (a phenomenon known as “the prozone effect”).1,4,9 Treponemal tests (TTs) include the FTA-ABS,T pallidumparticle agglutination assay,T pallidumenzyme immunoassay, and chemiluminescence immunoassay. These tests detect antibodies toT pallidumproteins and provide a qualitative result (either reactive or nonreactive). The sensitivity of the TT is 94.5% to 100% and specificity is 92% to 100%10; however, TTs may be nonreactive for up to 4 weeks after acute infection withT pallidum. In addition, because treponemal antibodies typically persist indefinitely after initial syphilis infection, TTs do not differentiate between a newly acquired or previously treated infection2,3,5(Figure). The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) 2024 recommendations for syphilis testing2endorsed both 2-step syphilis testing algorithms currently in practice—traditional and an alternative method termedreverse screening.3,6Traditional syphilis testing begins with a screening NTT, followed by a more specific TT. In the reverse testing algorithm, initial screening is performed with a TT and a positive test result is followed by a quantitative NTT (Supplement).The decision to use the traditional or reverse screening algorithm depends on laboratory testing volume, workflow, costs, and patient population.6In high-prevalence settings (eg, sexually transmitted infection clinics), the reverse algorithm is often preferred to minimize the risk of false negatives.6 According to the 2024Medicare fee schedule, reimbursement for NTTs (VDRL, RPR, and toluidine red unheated serum test) was $4.40 and TTs (FTA-ABS,T pallidumparticle agglutination assay,T pallidumenzyme immunoassay, and chemiluminescence immunoassay) was $13.24. The patient’s high-titer RPR (1:1024) at presentation made recent syphilis infection likely.7 Darkfield microscopy can directly detectT pallidumin lesion fluid, smears, and biopsy tissue, but is not commonly performed in the US due to limited availability of darkfield microscopes. Point-of-care (POC) testing for syphilis involves vertical flow immunoassays that are performed using a fingerstick or blood sample, provides results typically in less than 20 minutes, and often incorporates simultaneous HIV testing.1,9Although multiple POC tests are in use internationally, only 2 POC assays are currently approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Individuals with a positive POC test result should have NTT titer testing so that treatment response can be monitored. There are currently no FDA-approved nucleic acid amplification tests for syphilis testing. The patient’s FTA-ABS test results were positive and aT pallidumantibody immunohistochemical stain performed on a skin biopsy revealed numerous spirochetes. She was treated with 1 dose of intramuscular penicillin G (2.4 million units) and her test results were negative for HIV, hepatitis C, and hepatitis B. Eight weeks later, her rash had improved and her arthralgias and fatigue had resolved. She disclosed the diagnosis of syphilis to her sexual partner. At 6-month follow-up, her RPR was 1:256, a 4-fold decline that indicated treatment response and no reinfection.

scenario: A 36-year-old man presented for evaluation of elevated liver enzymes 2 months after undergoing a liver transplant for acute-on-chronic liver failure due to alcohol-associated hepatitis. He had metabolic comorbidities including obesity (body mass index of 30.6) and dyslipidemia. After the liver transplant, there was no evidence of organ rejection or biliary complications. He was asymptomatic and reported last alcohol use was prior to liver transplant. Vital signs were normal and physical examination revealed a well-healed abdominal surgical scar. Serum alcohol level was undetectable and urine drug screening results were positive for cannabinoids. Liver ultrasonography findings were normal. Liver biopsy showed 50% to 60% macrovesicular steatosis (normal <5%), mild portal inflammation, scattered apoptotic bodies, and hepatocyte ballooning (Table 1).

options.A: Acute rejection of the transplanted liver.
options.B: Alcohol-associated liver disease.

answer: Alcohol-associated liver disease.
distractors: Acute rejection of the transplanted liver.
Drug-induced liver injury.
Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease.
explanation: Phosphatidylethanol (PEth) is a whole blood marker of alcohol that can be detectable for up to 4 weeks after alcohol consumption. PEth is not a single molecule. It is a group of phospholipid homologues with a phosphoethanol head and 2 carboxylic acid side chains that attach to the erythrocyte surface in the presence of blood ethanol, catalyzed by the enzyme phospholipase D.1PEth species are categorized by the number of carbon atoms (typically 14-22) and double bonds; the 16:0/18:1 and 16:0/18:2 homologues are the most common forms.1Testing for PEth can be performed using dried blood spots or whole blood collected in ethylenediamine tetra-acetic acid tubes. PEth is a direct biomarker of alcohol that forms after ethanol consumption. A study of 16 recently abstinent volunteers who consumed alcohol to achieve a blood alcohol concentration of 1 g/kg (single ingestion of 110-230 mL of 40% vodka) demonstrated that PEth was detectable within 1 hour of alcohol consumption, peaked at 8 hours, and was detectable for 3 to 12 days after consumption, with a mean half-life of 3 days.2A PEth concentration less than 20 ng/mL indicates minimal or no recent alcohol consumption and a PEth concentration greater than 200 ng/mL correlates with heavy alcohol consumption (≥4 standard drinks daily). A standard drink is defined as equivalent to 12 fl oz of beer, 5 fl oz of wine, or 1.5 fl oz of distilled spirits.3 PEth formation and degradation are not affected by age, sex, or organ dysfunction such as chronic kidney disease or hepatic dysfunction.1The rate of PEth formation depends on the level and activity of phospholipase D, which varies among individuals. The degradation rate of PEth also varies, with an estimated mean half-life of 4 to 10 days. PEth may be detectable up to 5 weeks after heavy alcohol consumption.1Blood PEth level increases with higher quantity and frequency of alcohol consumption and decreases with time elapsed since last ingestion of alcohol. A false-positive PEth test result may occur if an individual receives a blood transfusion from a person who recently consumed alcohol, due to PEth on donated erythrocytes.4Falsely low PEth concentrations may occur in patients with low haptoglobin levels, consistent with intravascular hemolysis.5PEth has a sensitivity of 94.5% to 99% and a specificity of 100% for high levels of alcohol consumption (≥4 standard drinks daily) and a sensitivity of 81.8% for lower levels of alcohol ingestion.6In 2024, Medicare reimbursement was $114.43 for PEth testing.7 The patient’s PEth concentration of 137 ng/dL was consistent with recent alcohol ingestion despite his undetectable serum alcohol level and initial report of no recent alcohol consumption. Blood, breath, and urine alcohol levels detect alcohol consumed in the preceding 12 to 24 hours. Ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate are formed by enzymatic conjugation of ethanol with glucuronic acid and sulfate, respectively, and may be detected in urine within 2 to 3 hours of alcohol consumption and remain detectable for 4 to 5 days after consumption.8False-positive urinary ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate test results may occur due to kidney dysfunction or bacterial fermentation in the urine (eg, cystitis); false-negative results may occur with use of diuretics or intentional dilution of urine specimens.1Ethyl glucuronide can be detected in hair and nails for approximately 2 months after alcohol cessation in frequent drinkers9(Table 2).7,10Direct alcohol biomarkers (PEth and ethyl glucuronide) have been studied and validated in patients with and without liver disease. Additional testing revealed a urine ethyl sulfate level of 45 475 ng/mL (reference, <100 ng/mL) and urine ethyl glucuronide level of >10 000 ng/mL (reference, <500 ng/mL). The patient disclosed consuming 5 shots of vodka daily for 7 days prior to presentation. He was prescribed naltrexone and referred to an intensive outpatient program for alcohol use disorder. Liver chemistries were normal 2 weeks after presentation and PEth was undetectable 3 weeks later. In the clinic 2 months later, he reported alcohol abstinence; was meeting with his psychotherapy, psychiatry, and social work teams; and had undetectable blood PEth levels and normal liver graft function.

caption: Gingival enlargement at presentation and areas of recent gingival hemorrhage.
scenario: A 3-year-old previously healthy boy presented to the dental office for gum bleeding that developed 2 weeks prior to presentation. His parents reported dark spots on his gums that appeared spontaneously over several days and bleeding during teeth brushing. He had no preceding oral trauma and no recent infections. One week after onset of these oral symptoms, he developed a limp in the right leg. His parents also noticed he had difficulty standing up after sitting down to play. He was evaluated by a pediatrician, who diagnosed transient synovitis of the hip due to a viral infection. Findings on a radiograph of the right hip were normal. During the week prior to presentation, the patient developed spontaneous gingival bleeding and increased bilateral limb weakness with inability to bear weight. On presentation to the dental office, he appeared irritable. Physical examination revealed generalized gingival swelling and spontaneous gingival bleeding. He had no lesions on his lips and no edema or exudate in the oropharynx (Figure). The patient’s parents reported that he took no regular medications, had no recent use of aspirin or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications, and that his diet was limited to primarily chicken nuggets and milk.

options.A: Prescribe acyclovir (20 mg/kg) 4 times daily for 7 days
options.B: Prescribe amoxicillin (125 mg/5 mL oral suspension) for 7 days
options.D: Check plasma level of vitamin C

answer: Check plasma level of vitamin C
distractors: Prescribe acyclovir (20 mg/kg) 4 times daily for 7 days
Prescribe amoxicillin (125 mg/5 mL oral suspension) for 7 days
Perform a gingival biopsy
explanation: D. Check plasma level of vitamin C The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that spontaneous gingival hemorrhage and limb weakness are characteristic manifestations of scurvy. Herpes infection (choice A) is incorrect because this typically presents with vesicular lesions on the lips and is not associated with diffusely hemorrhagic gingiva. Amoxicillin (choice B) is not indicated because the patient’s symptoms are not suggestive of a bacterial infection. Biopsy of the gingiva (choice C) is an invasive procedure that should be considered only if plasma vitamin C level is within reference range. Vitamin C, also known as L-ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble nutrient that is important for fatty acid transport, neurotransmitter synthesis, prostaglandin metabolism, nitric oxide synthesis, and collagen synthesis.1,2Humans are unable to synthesize vitamin C, and it must be obtained through dietary intake.3Food sources of vitamin C include citrus fruits and vegetables (eg, broccoli, tomatoes, cauliflower, brussels sprouts).4Breast milk provides vitamin C to infants.2Vitamin C has a half-life of 10 to 20 days, and because humans are unable to store vitamin C, deficiency of vitamin C can develop within 1 to 3 months of inadequate vitamin C intake.2 Chronic vitamin C deficiency, also known as scurvy, is one of the oldest known nutritional disorders.4Although its exact incidence is unknown, scurvy is reported sporadically in the US in both children and adults; the 2017-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey estimated that 5.9% of the US population had vitamin C deficiency.2In high-income countries, scurvy may result from limited access to or inability to buy fruits and vegetables, or it may be associated with alcohol use disorder, eating disorders, and inflammatory bowel disease. Among children, risk factors include avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, autism, and neglect.2,5Infants who are exclusively fed cow’s milk are also at increased risk of scurvy.2 Initial signs of scurvy include loss of appetite, low-grade fever, and agitation,6typically followed by generalized gingival swelling and spontaneous bleeding.4Dermatologic features include petechiae, ecchymosis, perifollicular hemorrhage, and corkscrew hair.2Scurvy may cause periodontal disease, loosening of teeth within their sockets, and loss of teeth.4Musculoskeletal symptoms such as arthralgia of the knee, wrist, or ankle; myalgia; and asthenia develop in approximately 80% of patients with scurvy.7The most common radiographic feature of scurvy is Frankel sign, consisting of increased calcification around the metaphysis.7 Symptoms of scurvy typically occur when plasma vitamin C levels are less than 0.2 mg/dL (reference, 0.6-2.0 mg/dL), although recent vitamin C intake can result in normal plasma levels even if tissue levels are low.8Prompt resolution of symptoms after treatment with vitamin C is the best indicator of the diagnosis of scurvy.4Laboratory evaluation reveals anemia in 75% of patients with scurvy,5and values for inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated.9The differential diagnosis includes osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, systemic lupus erythematosus, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, disseminated intravascular coagulation, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, and child neglect or abuse.4,7,9Diagnosis is commonly delayed; in 9 studies of 42 children with scurvy, the median time from onset of clinical symptoms to diagnosis of scurvy was 2 months.10A high index of suspicion is necessary to promptly diagnose scurvy. If untreated, scurvy can cause dyspnea, hypotension, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and sudden death.2 Although there are no established treatment guidelines, initial therapy typically involves oral, intramuscular, or intravenous administration of high-dose vitamin C (300-1000 mg daily) for several days to 1 week, followed by 100 to 300 mg daily for 1 month.2,3,5Three-times-daily dosing of vitamin C is recommended to maximize intestinal absorption.10After initial treatment, a diet that contains sufficient fresh fruits and vegetables can prevent recurrence of scurvy. The patient’s vitamin C level was undetectable. He started oral vitamin C, 600 mg/d. Within 48 hours, his parents reported resolution of gingival bleeding and improved muscle strength. Two weeks after starting vitamin C, the patient’s gingiva, muscle strength, and gait were normal. He is taking a multivitamin supplement daily, and his parents have incorporated more fruits and vegetables into his diet.

scenario: A 41-year-old man with type 1 diabetes and a hemoglobin A1clevel of 16.8% (reference, 4.0%-5.6%) 1 month prior to admission presented to the emergency department with 1 week of generalized weakness. His temperature was 38.5 °C (101.3 °F); blood pressure, 125/75 mm Hg; heart rate, 95/min; respiratory rate, 24/min; and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. His voice was muffled and his speech was dysarthric. He appeared lethargic but had no focal neurologic deficits. Physical examination findings were normal except for tonsillar edema. White blood cell count was 13.4 ×103/μL (reference, 4-11 ×103/μL); blood glucose level, 274 mg/dL (15.21 mmol/L) (reference, 70-100 mg/dL [3.89-5.55 mmol/L]); serum creatinine level, 0.9 mg/dL (79.56 μmol/L) (reference, 0.4-1.3 mg/dL [35.36-114.92 μmol/L]); bicarbonate level, 9 mmol/L (reference, 20-30 mmol/L); arterial pH, 7.21 (reference, 7.35-7.45); β-hydroxybutyric acid level, 58.2 mg/dL (5590 μmol/L) (reference, <2.81 mg/dL [269.9 μmol/L]); and serum anion gap, 21 (reference, 7-17). explanation: A. Initiate liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that the nonseptate right-angled hyphae present in the sinus mucosal biopsy sample are diagnostic of mucormycosis. Obtaining a serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan level (choice B) would not be helpful because it detects a fungal cell wall component that is absent in mucormycetes. Fluconazole (choice C) is not recommended because it is inactive against fungi that cause mucormycosis. Steroids (choice D) are contraindicated because they may increase the invasiveness of nasopharyngeal mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is a disease caused by a heterogeneous group of more than 250 fungal species.Rhizopus,Mucor,Lichtheimia, andRhizomucorare the most frequent human pathogens1and are present worldwide.2Rhino-orbital-cerebral infection is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis, although other organs such as the lung, intestines, and skin can become infected.2,3Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis typically enters the body through inhalation of spores that deposit in the nasopharynx or through penetrating trauma.2It is a rapidly progressive infection that can involve the brain and is associated with a mortality rate of 25% to 62%.2-4Patients at highest risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis are those with poorly controlled diabetes, high serum iron levels (eg, hemochromatosis), and prolonged neutropenia or impaired cellular immunity (eg, hematologic malignancies; solid organ or bone marrow transplants).2,3SARS-CoV-2 infection is also associated with rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, especially among patients treated with steroids who develop hyperglycemia.5National epidemiology studies are lacking, but 1 study estimated the annual incidence of mucormycosis at 3 cases/million individuals in the US.6 Patients with mucormycosis may present with orbital swelling, facial pain, proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, headache, acute vision loss, and, in severe cases, a facial necrotic eschar. Among immunosuppressed patients, the primary differential diagnosis is invasive fungal rhinosinusitis due toAspergillus. The diagnosis of mucormycosis is based on histopathology, which shows characteristic nonseptate right-angled hyphae often appearing in “ribbon formations,”3angioinvasion and infarction of surrounding tissue, and, rarely, fruiting bodies, the morphologically distinctive spore-producing component of the fungus. Staining and culture of tissues containing fungus7can help identify fungal species and identify antimicrobial susceptibility. Polymerase chain reaction testing of tissue specimens may be used to identify the specific fungus when histopathology is consistent with mucormycosis but a fungal culture result is negative.3,8 Patients with rhino-orbital-cerebral disease who have risk factors for mucormycosis (eg, uncontrolled diabetes, immunosuppression) need prompt evaluation and surgical debridement of all infected tissue. First-line treatment for rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is liposomal amphotericin B, which should be administered promptly after diagnosis is suspected and is typically prescribed for 4 to 6 weeks, although duration of therapy depends on clinical improvement and the level of immunosuppression. Oral isavuconazole and posaconazole are less effective medications but may be used if liposomal amphotericin B is contraindicated; they may be coadministered with liposomal amphotericin B in patients with severe disease or may be prescribed as step-down therapy after improvement with liposomal amphotericin B.3 The patient was treated empirically with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B beginning intraoperatively. One week later, the result of an 18s rRNA gene-based polymerase chain reaction test performed on sinus mucosal biopsy tissue was positive for theRhizopus oryzaecomplex. Repeat fiberoptic laryngoscopy on postoperative day 1 revealed no residual necrotic tissue but identified new vocal cord paralysis, for which the patient underwent an elective tracheostomy and placement of a gastrostomy tube 2 days after his initial surgery. He underwent decannulation 2 months later and was discharged home after a 65-day hospitalization, during which he was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily for 4 weeks) and then transitioned to oral posaconazole (delayed-release, 300 mg daily). At follow-up 1 week after discharge, he reported no significant concerns other than some difficulty with phonation. He was instructed to continue posaconazole for an additional 3 months.

scenario: A 43-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of recurring symptoms of sudden onset of fatigue, palpitations, dyspnea, chest pain, lightheadedness, and nausea that were associated with standing and resolved with sitting. These symptoms began 1 month after mild COVID-19 infection. At presentation, while supine, blood pressure (BP) was 123/70 mm Hg and heart rate (HR) was 90/min; while seated, BP was 120/80 and HR was 93/min; after standing for 1 minute, BP was 124/80 and HR was 119/min. Physical examination results were normal. Oxygen saturation was 98% at rest while breathing room air. She had no oxygen desaturation during a 6-minute walk test but walked only 282 m (45% predicted). Complete blood cell count, morning cortisol, and thyrotropin blood levels were normal. Electrocardiogram (ECG), chest computed tomography, pulmonary function testing, methacholine challenge, bronchoscopy, echocardiography, and cardiac catheterization findings were normal. During tilt table testing, the patient experienced lightheadedness and nausea when moved from horizontal to the upright position. Results of the tilt table test are shown in theTableandFigure.

options.A: Normal tilt table test results
options.B: Orthostatic hypotension

answer: Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS)
distractors: Normal tilt table test results
Orthostatic hypotension
Panic disorder with hyperventilation
explanation: D. Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) Tilt table testing is performed in the inpatient or outpatient setting and measures an individual’s symptoms and hemodynamic response to the downward displacement of intravascular volume with movement from the supine to upright position. During tilt table testing, movement from horizontal to upright positioning normally provokes an increase in sympathetic adrenergic outflow to sustain cardiac output. A normal response is a mild decrease in BP (decline in systolic BP <20 mm Hg and decline in diastolic BP <10 mm Hg) and a mild increase in HR (increase of <30/min). Tilt table testing can be used to evaluate patients who have syncope of unknown cause, suspected vasovagal or orthostatic syncope, and/or autonomic dysfunction, including orthostatic hypotension and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS). Prior to tilt table testing, patients are instructed to abstain from alcohol and caffeine for 12 hours and to fast for at least 2 hours. During testing, individuals lie horizontally on a padded table with lateral armrests that position the arms at the level of the heart. Adjustable nonconstricting straps secure the chest and legs. Patients are monitored with continuous ECG. Brachial artery systolic pressure is measured at 1-minute intervals with sphygmomanometry, and finger-cuff photoplethysmography can be used for continuous beat-to-beat BP monitoring. After the patient rests supine for at least 10 minutes, the motorized table moves into a 70° incline within 10 seconds. Throughout the test, patients report any symptoms. The duration of tilt table testing ranges from 5 to 10 minutes for patients with suspected orthostatic intolerance to 30 to 45 minutes for patients undergoing evaluation for vasovagal syncope. False-positive results occur in 10% to 15% of asymptomatic control individuals.1,2The sensitivity of tilt table testing is difficult to assess because there is no accepted criterion standard, and there may be protocol variability among centers performing this test.1-4 Tilt table testing is contraindicated in pregnant individuals and in those with severe coronary artery or cerebrovascular disease because hypotension may precipitate myocardial or cerebral ischemia. Medicare reimbursement for tilt table testing in 2023 was approximately $370.5 During tilt table testing, the patient’s BP was stable and her HR increased more than 30/min above her baseline HR during minutes 3 through 10 of testing, reaching a peak of 42/min above baseline. The hemodynamic finding of increased HR without simultaneous hypotension is characteristic of POTS, defined as chronic orthostatic intolerance for at least 3 months with a sustained HR increase of 30/min or more above baseline (40/min for patients aged 8-19 years) that occurs within 10 minutes of standing up or head-up tilt, without simultaneous hypotension.6POTS develops in approximately 1% of people after COVID-19 infection,7and in 15% to 20% of patients with post–COVID-19 condition (long COVID).8-10 Orthostatic vital signs involves measuring BP and HR after patients lie supine for at least 5 minutes, and then at 1, 3, and sometimes 5 minutes after standing. Compared to tilt table testing, active standing typically causes a greater initial transient rise in HR. The patient was treated with midodrine, 7.5 mg 3 times daily, pyridostigmine, 60 mg 3 times daily, and ivabradine, 2.5 mg twice daily. She was instructed to increase salt intake to 5 to 10 g/d, drink fluids up to 2 to 3 L/d, and wear lower extremity compressive garments. She began a progressive exercise program that included lower extremity strength training. At 3 years after COVID-19 infection, her symptoms of fatigue and palpitations, dyspnea, and chest pain when standing were improved. She had returned to work part-time, could walk for 20 minutes, and exercised on a stationary bicycle for 10 minutes twice weekly.

caption: Oral examination showing plaques on the oral mucosa and thickened buccal mucosae.
scenario: A 63-year-old woman presented to the clinic with intermittent pain inside her mouth and a progressive decline in oral aperture that had developed over the prior year. She described a burning sensation inside her mouth that worsened with using mouthwash and eating spicy foods. She had no history of cigarette smoking or use of chewing tobacco but had chewed areca nuts for many years while living in India. Currently, she reported chewing areca nuts daily to weekly. Physical examination revealed white-tan plaques on the oral mucosa and thickened buccal mucosae bilaterally (Figure). Her lips and perioral skin appeared healthy, and the interincisal distance, defined as the distance between the tips of the frontal incisors when the mouth is opened as wide as possible, was approximately 25 mm (reference, >35 mm). Examination of a biopsy sample of the lower left labial mucosa revealed subepithelial fibrosis with stromal hyalinization, without epithelial dysplasia or inflammatory changes.

options.A: Apply topical clobetasol (0.05% twice daily) to the oral mucosa
options.B: Recommend cessation of areca nut use

answer: Recommend cessation of areca nut use
distractors: Apply topical clobetasol (0.05% twice daily) to the oral mucosa
Refer to oral physical therapy
Start omeprazole (20 mg daily)
explanation: B. Recommend cessation of areca nut use The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that burning and pain in the mouth, reduced oral aperture, and subepithelial fibrosis on biopsy are characteristic of oral submucous fibrosis (OSMF), which is associated with chewing areca nuts.1Although topical steroids (choice A) may occasionally be prescribed for patients with OSMF, first-line therapy is cessation of areca nut chewing. While oral physical therapy (choice C) may be prescribed for patients with OSMF, it is insufficient without cessation of areca nut chewing. This patient did not have symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux, so initiation of a proton pump inhibitor (choice D) was not indicated. OSMF is a chronic disabling disorder of the oral mucosa characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the oral mucosa (lamina propria and deeper tissue) and is primarily caused by chewing of areca nuts.2,3Areca nut is the seed ofAreca catechu, a species of palm tree, that grows in the tropical Pacific, Asia, and East Africa.2More than 600 million people, primarily in Asia and in Asian migrant communities around the world, chew areca nuts, and use is highest among adolescents and adults younger than 40 years.4A common preparation is betel quid, which combines areca nuts with betel leaves and other ingredients, including chewing tobacco.2,4Chewing areca nuts causes mild euphoria but has addictive potential and may be associated with withdrawal symptoms such as irritability and anxiety.2 The areca nut is designated as a type-1 carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer.2,5Chewing areca nuts causes abrasion and inflammation of the oral mucosa, which allows areca nut components to penetrate the oral mucosa.3,6Alkaloids in areca nuts promote collagen synthesis, resulting in oral mucosal fibrosis.3,6,7Areca nuts are thought to promote malignancy by upregulatingp53, hypoxia-inducible factor 1α, and other angiogenesis-related molecules.3,7 In 2022, the global prevalence of OSMF was approximately 4.96%.6Increased risk of OSMF may occur in people who chew areca nuts and also chew or smoke tobacco and in those who regularly eat spicy chilis or have heavy alcohol consumption, high copper intake, or deficiencies in iron, folate, and vitamin B12.6,8Patients with OSMF often report oral burning and pain and may have tongue depapillation, blanching or leathery oral mucosa, and oral ulcerations and vesicles.1,8The interincisal mouth opening is reduced to 20 to 35 mm in patients with moderate OSMF and to less than 20 mm in those with severe OSMF.1Individuals with advanced-stage OSMF may report weight loss, trismus, dysphonia, or hearing impairment.8Patients with OSMF are at increased risk of developing oral squamous cell carcinoma, with rates estimated at 7% to 30%.1 The differential diagnosis of OSMF includes other oral potential premalignant disorders (such as leukoplakia, erythroplakia, and actinic cheilitis), amyloidosis, generalized fibromatosis, scleroderma, and oral lichen planus.9Diagnosis is made through an oral mucosal biopsy that shows dense subepithelial fibrosis, hyalinization of collagen, and decreased density of dermal blood vessels, sometimes accompanied by an atrophic or hypertrophic epidermis.7However, in countries with limited resources, OSMF is often diagnosed based on a history of areca nut chewing and characteristic clinical findings.1,6Oral mucosal biopsy is recommended for patients with leukoplakia or erythroplakia or for those with an oral ulcer persisting longer than 3 weeks, to evaluate for dysplasia and oral squamous cell carcinoma.1 Although OSMF is irreversible, cessation of areca nut chewing decreases its progression and reduces the risk of oral squamous cell carcinoma. Educational and behavioral interventions for cessation of areca nut chewing have been successful in randomized clinical trials.5,10Patients should be encouraged to not smoke or chew tobacco, to decrease alcohol intake, and to correct nutritional deficiencies. Oral physical therapy,1which involves mouth opening exercises or fibrous band massage, may be helpful for patients with reduced oral aperture due to OSMF.1,3,6Although there are no randomized clinical trials of treatments for OSMF, corticosteroids applied topically or injected into areas of oral fibrosis may reduce oral discomfort.8Surgical excision of fibrotic bands and reconstruction with tissue flaps may be considered for patients with advanced OSMF.1,5,6 The patient stopped chewing areca nuts 1 month after presentation to the dermatology clinic. She is undergoing evaluation every 6 months by an oral pathologist for abnormalities suggestive of squamous cell carcinoma. When seen in clinic approximately 1 year after initial presentation, she had not resumed chewing areca nuts. Her oral symptoms were stable, and oral examination revealed no progression of OSMF.

scenario: A 69-year-old man presented to the rheumatology clinic 3 weeks after being hospitalized for fever, fatigue, rash, right periorbital swelling, and shortness of breath. This was his fifth inpatient stay in the past 3 years for similar symptoms. During a recent hospitalization, he had purpuric macules and plaques on his lower extremities bilaterally (Figure, left panel). Laboratory testing revealed a white blood cell count of 2.9 × 103/μL (reference, 4.2-10.8 ×103/μL); mean corpuscular volume, 96.1 fL (reference, 80-96 fL); hemoglobin level, 12.4 mg/dL (reference, 14.0-18.0 mg/dL); and a normal platelet count. C-reactive protein level was 270 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 98 mm/h (reference, 0-20 mm/h).Results of testing for antinuclear antibody and antineutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibodies were negative. Computed tomography of the chest revealed numerous small, bilateral pulmonary nodules (Figure, right panel). Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed bilateral inferior rectus muscle enlargement with mild inflammatory changes along the extraocular muscles and optic nerves. A skin biopsy showed a perivascular neutrophilic infiltrate consistent with leukocytoclastic vasculitis. During his most recent hospitalization, he was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone (40 mg twice daily) for 5 days and discharged taking oral prednisone (40 mg daily) for 4 weeks. Previously, he had pericardial and pleural effusions and pulmonary infiltrates. Pericardial biopsy showed organizing pericarditis and lung biopsy revealed cryptogenic organizing pneumonia, with negative IgG4 stains. Results of bone marrow biopsy, including flow cytometry and cytogenetic testing, performed 18 months prior to the current presentation were normal. At presentation, his temperature was 36.4 °C (97.5 °F); blood pressure, 149/66 mm Hg; heart rate, 90/min; and oxygen saturation, 98% on room air. Physical examination findings were normal.

options.B: Measure plasma adenosine deaminase 2 (ADA2) activity
options.C: Order serum anticollagen type II antibody levels

answer: Perform testing for ubiquitin-like modifier activating enzyme 1 (UBA1) gene variants.

explanation: VEXAS (vacuoles, E1-ubiquitin-activating enzyme, X-linked, autoinflammatory, somatic) syndrome D. Perform testing for ubiquitin-like modifier activating enzyme 1 (UBA1) gene variants. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that recurrent episodes of fever and inflammation affecting skin, lungs, and other organs, and macrocytic anemia, are characteristic of VEXAS syndrome. Choice A is not recommended because IL-18 is a nonspecific marker of inflammation. Choice B is incorrect because this patient did not have peripheral vasculopathy and stroke, which are characteristic of ADA2 deficiency. Choice C would not be useful because anticollagen II antibody levels are elevated in several inflammatory diseases. First reported in 2020, VEXAS syndrome is a rare disease caused by aUBA1gene variant in hematopoietic progenitor cells.1﻿UBA1gene variants reduce function of theUBA1enzyme, which facilitates protein ubiquitination, a posttranslational modification process essential for cell signaling and protein degradation. Patients with VEXAS syndrome experience autoinflammation, characterized by recurrent episodes of inflammation in various organs.2 UBA1gene variants are X-linked, so VEXAS syndrome has been reported only in men, or in women with monosomy of the X chromosome (Turner syndrome).3As a somatic gene variant, it is not inherited, and VEXAS syndrome predominantly affects people older than 50 years.4The prevalence of VEXAS syndrome is uncertain. A recent study of exome sequencing on DNA extracted from peripheral blood reported that 1 in 4269 men older than 50 years had aUBA1variant associated with VEXAS syndrome, although not all patients had symptoms of VEXAS syndrome.4 Clinical manifestations of VEXAS syndrome are variable and include skin lesions (eg, cutaneous vasculitis, neutrophilic dermatoses, erythema nodosum), recurrent fever, weight loss, orchitis, hepatosplenomegaly, ocular manifestations (eg, orbital inflammation, uveitis, scleritis, episcleritis), sensorineural hearing loss, and inflammatory arthritis.2,5Approximately 40% to 60% of patients develop thromboembolism, and up to 77% have pulmonary infiltrates on computed tomography scans.6Patients with VEXAS syndrome also have frequently been diagnosed with Sweet syndrome, giant cell arteritis, polyarteritis nodosa, relapsing polychondritis, myelodysplastic syndromes, and multiple myeloma.1-3,5VEXAS syndrome should be considered in men with late-onset, undiagnosed inflammatory syndromes with associated hematologic abnormalities. Elevated inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein level, erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and macrocytic anemia are typical laboratory findings. Lymphopenia occurs in approximately 80% and thrombocytopenia in 50% of patients with VEXAS syndrome.2On bone marrow biopsy, more than 10% cytoplasmic vacuoles in myeloid and erythroid precursor cells is an indication forUB1Atesting.2The diagnosis of VEXAS syndrome is made by identifyingUBA1gene variants with polymerase chain reaction–based sequencing of DNA extracted from peripheral blood, bone marrow, or formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue in a patient with symptoms characteristic of VEXAS syndrome.7,8 In the absence of rigorous trials, corticosteroids are typically first-line treatment. Trials of steroid-sparing agents such as tocilizumab, azacitidine, Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors, and allogeneic stem cell transplant have included very small numbers of patients and have produced variable results with high rates of adverse events (eg, pneumonia, thromboembolism). Therefore, treatment should be individualized.9,10 Patients diagnosed with VEXAS syndrome have a 5-year survival of approximately 63%,6and those with the p.Met41Val variant had a median survival of 9 years after symptom onset.8 A polymerase chain reaction–based next-generation sequencing of DNA from the patient’s prior bone marrow specimen identified a pathogenicUBA1gene variant,UBA1c.121A>G (p.Met41Val), confirming the diagnosis of VEXAS syndrome. In addition to prednisone (20 mg) daily, the patient was prescribed weekly subcutaneous tocilizumab (162 mg), which was discontinued after 4 months due to leukopenia and recurrent cutaneous vasculitis on his legs. The patient did not want to enroll in a clinical trial and declined evaluation for allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Ten months after presentation, he was taking prednisone (15 mg) daily and his physical examination findings were normal.
