scenario: A 46-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 3 months of upper back pain and 2 weeks of dry cough and subjective fevers that did not improve with empirical azithromycin. He had immigrated from India to the US 15 years prior and worked as a software engineer. He last traveled to India 4 years earlier and had negative results for interferon gamma release assay on return. He reported no smoking history, recent animal contact, or unpasteurized animal product ingestion. His temperature was 38.05 °C; heart rate, 114/min; blood pressure, 132/85 mm Hg; and respiratory rate, 18/min. There was no spinal or paraspinal tenderness. Findings on pulmonary and neurologic examinations were normal. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 84 mm/h (reference, <10 mm/h), and C-reactive protein level was 9.4 mg/dL (reference, <0.8 mg/dL). A chest radiograph showed prominent reticular markings in the left perihilar area, and chest computed tomography showed a 3.2 × 2.6–cm dense consolidation in the left lower lobe (Figure 1, left panel). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spine showed signal abnormality and extensive contrast enhancement within the T6, T7, and T8 vertebral bodies, with sparing of the T6-7 and T7-8 disks (Figure 1, center panel), and a large paraspinal soft tissue mass with spinal cord compression (Figure 1, center and right panel).

options.A: Place the patient in airborne isolation and begin ethambutol, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and rifampin
options.B: Measure prostate-specific antigen level

answer: Place the patient in airborne isolation and begin ethambutol, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and rifampin
distractors: Measure prostate-specific antigen level
Start cefepime and vancomycin
Start doxycycline, rifampin, and streptomycin
explanation: A. Place the patient in airborne isolation and begin ethambutol, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and rifampin The keys to the correct diagnosis were MRI findings of a paraspinal mass with signal abnormality and extensive contrast enhancement in the lower thoracic vertebral bodies and relative sparing of the intervertebral disks (consistent with Pott disease), along with fever, cough, and consolidation on chest computed tomography in a patient who had traveled to a country with a high prevalence of tuberculosis.1The combination of ethambutol, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and rifampin (choice A) is first-line treatment for drug-susceptible tuberculosis. Cefepime and vancomycin (choice C) would be appropriate empirical antibiotics for bacterial vertebral osteomyelitis, characterized by contrast enhancement of the vertebral bodies along with signal abnormalities within the intervertebral disks. Empirical therapy forBrucellaspondylitis (choice D) could be considered if there was exposure to animals or unpasteurized animal products. Metastatic spinal tumors are included in the differential diagnosis of multiple spinal lesions on MRI, particularly in the absence of disk involvement; however, osteoblastic metastases from prostate cancer (choice B) do not enhance on MRI and are characterized by very-low-signal intensities in all sequences. Vertebral osteomyelitis and intervertebral diskitis caused byMycobacterium tuberculosisare termedtuberculous spondylitisorPott disease. Of 8916 cases of tuberculosis reported in 2019 in the US, 1833 (20.6%) were extrapulmonary. Of these, 164 (8.4%) involved osteoarticular infection.2Pott disease accounts for approximately half of osteoarticular tuberculosis.3,4Pott disease is associated with concomitant pulmonary tuberculosis in approximately 20% of patients.4 Pott disease has an indolent course. Back discomfort is reported by approximately 80% of patients and may be the only initial symptom.3,5,6Systemic signs of illness (ie, fever, night sweats, and weight loss) occur in fewer than half of patients.3,5,6Delay in diagnosis is typical. In a multinational cohort study of 314 patients, median duration from symptom onset to diagnosis was 78 days.3,6Adjacent lower thoracic or lumbar vertebrae are most commonly affected. The cervical or upper thoracic spine are involved in fewer than 10% of patients.3,6The intervertebral disk space is affected later in the disease course compared with other causes of vertebral osteomyelitis; thus, relative disk sparing is a characteristic radiologic feature of Pott disease.1,7A paraspinal mass, termed acold abscess, which lacks erythema, tenderness, and warmth, occurs in about 50% of patients.6The paraspinal mass can impinge on the spinal cord. Neurologic deficits occur in approximately 40% of patients at diagnosis.3,6,7 The optimal treatment duration for Pott disease is unclear. For rifampin-containing regimens, 85% to 98% of participants in randomized trials who received 6 or 9 months of therapy gained full physical activity with no clinical or radiographic evidence of active disease at 5-year follow-up.8Many experts extend treatment to 12 months in the presence of orthopedic hardware or when treatment response is difficult to follow.9Surgical intervention is reserved for patients with spinal instability or neurologic deficits.8,9 The diagnosis was confirmed with positive sputum nucleic acid amplification testing results forM tuberculosis. Sputum smear for acid-fast bacilli, which has 50% to 80% sensitivity for active pulmonary tuberculosis, was negative. Histopathology of the paraspinal mass showed necrotizing granulomas with rare acid-fast bacilli (Figure 2). Cultures of both the mass and sputum grewM tuberculosissusceptible to all first-line medications. The patient was likely infected during travel to India 4 years prior, and the negative findings on subsequent interferon gamma release assay were likely a result of recent infection or anergy to tuberculosis antigen.10Fevers improved after several days of treatment and his neurologic examination remained normal. At most recent follow-up, 2.5 months after initiating antituberculosis medications, back pain was improved but not resolved.

scenario: A 50-year-old woman with a history of seizures presented to the electromyography laboratory with progressive lower extremity pain and gait imbalance for approximately 5 years. A neurological examination demonstrated reduced pinprick sensation in both feet and absent vibratory sensation at the first toes. Mild weakness of ankle dorsiflexion and absent ankle jerk reflexes were noted bilaterally. She had a slightly wide-based gait, high-arched feet, and hammer toes. She had no known family history of polyneuropathy and no history of diabetes, alcohol misuse, known vitamin deficiency, hypothyroidism, or HIV. Nerve conduction studies (NCS) and needle electromyography (EMG) were performed. The results are shown inTable 1andTable 2.

options.A: Results are consistent with axonal polyneuropathy
options.B: Results are consistent with demyelinating polyneuropathy

answer: Results are consistent with axonal polyneuropathy
distractors: Results are consistent with demyelinating polyneuropathy
Results are consistent with polyradiculopathy
Results are normal
explanation: A. Results are consistent with axonal polyneuropathy Electrodiagnostic testing typically includes NCS and needle EMG. NCS involves application of an electrical stimulus to the skin above a nerve and use of surface electrodes to record waveform responses from individual sensory and motor nerves. The action potential generated after electrical stimulation represents the number of fibers depolarized. The amplitude, distal latency, and conduction velocity of an action potential help distinguish whether a neuropathy is axonal or demyelinating. Needle EMG involves placement of a small recording needle electrode into a muscle to evaluate for abnormal insertional activity or spontaneous activity upon needle insertion and to assess voluntary motor units with volitional activation of the muscle. EMG can help distinguish neurogenic or myopathic weakness.1 Definitive assessment of the sensitivity and specificity of NCS for detection of polyneuropathy is difficult due to the lack of a criterion standard. A study of 313 patients with confirmed polyneuropathy 1 to 6 years after NCS testing reported that surface sural NCS recordings had a sensitivity of 49% and specificity of 100%.2Medicare reimbursement for electrodiagnostic testing, including both NCS and EMG, typically ranges from $190.48 to $371.26.3However, the extent of electrodiagnostic testing depends on a patient’s distribution of symptoms, so costs may vary. Electrodiagnostic testing may be used to diagnose polyneuropathy, which is typically characterized by distal and symmetric abnormalities of sensory and motor nerve function. Polyneuropathy affects approximately 15% of individuals in the US older than 40 years, with diabetes being the most common cause.4Electrodiagnostic testing can help delineate whether a neuropathy is axonal, which is characterized by direct injury to and loss of axons, or demyelinating, which involves damage to the myelin sheath surrounding nerve fibers. Axonal polyneuropathy typically results in low-amplitude or absent sensory or motor nerve responses on NCS findings, whereas demyelinating polyneuropathy presents with prolonged latencies or slowed conduction velocities. Certain abnormalities on needle EMG results in patients with polyneuropathy may suggest active or chronic denervation associated with the neuropathy.5An EMG test may also be helpful to evaluate for radiculopathy.6 Results of the NCS showed that the patient had an absent sural sensory response and decreased amplitudes of the peroneal motor and radial sensory responses (Table 1). These abnormalities are consistent with a severe sensory and motor polyneuropathy, characterized by axonal loss rather than demyelination, because the predominant abnormality is the low amplitude of the affected nerves rather than slowed conduction velocities. The patient’s polyneuropathy appeared length-dependent, meaning the nerve endings in the feet were affected before the hands, as shown by the results of sural sensory and peroneal motor studies being substantially more abnormal than the ulnar motor and radial sensory studies. Results of the needle EMG showed changes in voluntary motor unit morphology and a reduction in the recruitment pattern of the voluntary motor units in the first dorsal interosseous and tibialis anterior muscles, consistent with a severe degree of chronic reinnervation. The patient’s electrodiagnostic test findings, coupled with her abnormal foot appearance, raised the clinical suspicion for an underlying hereditary neuropathy. If the diagnosis of polyneuropathy is highly likely based on a patient’s medical history (eg, diabetes, chemotherapy exposure), electrodiagnostic testing may not be necessary because it will not change the clinical management. If Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease or another hereditary sensory and motor neuropathy is strongly suspected, a patient with polyneuropathy may directly undergo genetic testing instead of proceeding first with electrodiagnostic testing. Due to her severe axonal polyneuropathy and abnormal foot morphology in the absence of other common causes for polyneuropathy, genetic testing for Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease was performed, which revealed a pathogenic variant inMFN2(Mitofusin 2). Variants in this gene are a common cause of axonal Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease7-9and may result in a mild and late-onset presentation of sensory and motor neuropathy.10Obtaining the diagnosis of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is important for appropriate genetic counseling, symptomatic treatment, and avoidance of additional, unnecessary tests.

scenario: An 18-year-old woman with no significant medical history and no history of sexual intercourse presented for evaluation of pharyngitis and tonsillar exudates of 1 week duration. She reported neck swelling and an occasional dry cough but no fevers, chills, trismus, headache, dyspnea, chest pain, abdominal pain, fatigue, or rash. One week prior to presentation, she visited an urgent care clinic for evaluation of pharyngitis and white exudates on her tonsils. Results of a rapid strep test and heterophile antibody test (monospot) were negative. A throat culture was obtained and she was prescribed amoxicillin (500 mg twice daily for 10 days) for possible group A streptococcal infection. Despite taking antibiotics for 7 days, she had no improvement in her symptoms. One day prior to presentation, the urgent care clinic notified the patient that her throat culture results were negative. On presentation, the patient was in no acute distress and had normal vital signs. She had bilateral white tonsillar exudates and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, but no exudate was observed elsewhere in the oral cavity and the uvula was midline (Figure). There was no axillary or inguinal adenopathy and no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. The remainder of the physical examination was normal.

options.A: Obtain an ultrasound of the neck
options.B: Prescribe azithromycin
options.C: Recheck a rapid heterophile antibody test
options.D: Treat with an oral antifungal medication

answer: Recheck a rapid heterophile antibody test
distractors: Obtain an ultrasound of the neck
Prescribe azithromycin
Treat with an oral antifungal medication
explanation: C. Recheck a rapid heterophile antibody test The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that infectious mononucleosis can present without constitutional symptoms of fever and fatigue and that a rapid heterophile antibody test result may be falsely negative early in the illness. Obtaining an ultrasound of the neck (choice A) is incorrect because peritonsillar abscess is unlikely without fever, trismus, and uvula deviation. Prescribing azithromycin (choice B) is inappropriate. Moreover, an antibiotic should not have been prescribed initially by the urgent care center because this patient had a negative rapid strep test result and had only 2 of 4 Centor criteria1for streptococcal pharyngitis. The tonsillar exudates were present before starting antibiotics and no abnormalities were noted on the tongue, so thrush is unlikely and therefore treatment with an antifungal medication (choice D) is not recommended. Infectious mononucleosis is a syndrome caused by a viral infection that typically presents with the triad of fever, lymphadenopathy, and pharyngitis. Fatigue, splenomegaly, and atypical lymphocytosis of greater than or equal to 10% are also common features of infectious mononucleosis.2However, some patients have relatively mild disease, presenting only with oropharyngotonsillitis. Others may have fever and lymphadenopathy without pharyngitis. Infectious mononucleosis in adults older than 40 years is less likely to present with lymphadenopathy and pharyngitis and more likely to be associated with prolonged fevers, hepatitis, cholestasis, and hepatomegaly.3 Approximately 90% of infectious mononucleosis diagnoses are caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a member of the herpesvirus family. The remainder are caused by cytomegalovirus, human herpesvirus 6, and acute HIV. EBV infection is common, with more than 95% of all adults worldwide estimated to be seropositive for EBV.4EBV is typically transmitted person-to-person via exposure to infected saliva through kissing, sharing of food or drink, coughing, and, less commonly, through sexual transmission. Rarely, EBV can be transmitted by blood transfusion, solid organ transplant, or hematopoietic stem cell transplant.5The incubation period between viral infection and symptom onset is typically 4 to 8 weeks. Infectious mononucleosis presents most commonly in teenagers and young adults in high-income countries. In developing countries, EBV infection tends to occur in early childhood and is often asymptomatic or presents as a nonspecific illness.6Older adults are less likely to develop infectious mononucleosis because of immunity acquired from EBV infection earlier in life. The differential diagnosis for the infectious mononucleosis triad of fever, lymphadenopathy, and pharyngitis includes infection with group A streptococcus, toxoplasma gondii, lymphoma, or drug reaction to certain anticonvulsant medications or antibiotics. Diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis is typically performed by demonstration of heterophile antibodies, which develop in response to infection with EBV and can be detected with rapid diagnostic tests using a latex agglutination assay or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay technique. The sensitivity of rapid tests for heterophile antibodies is estimated at 70% to 92% and specificity as 96% to 100%,7but false-negatives occur in approximately 25% of patients with infectious mononucleosis within the first week of infection.8If the result of a rapid test for heterophile antibodies is negative early in the course of illness and suspicion for infectious mononucleosis remains high, the rapid test should be repeated, EBV-specific antibodies can be obtained, or both. No antiviral medications are effective against infectious mononucleosis. Most patients with infectious mononucleosis recover from pharyngitis within 1 to 2 weeks. Fatigue typically lasts several weeks beyond the resolution of pharyngitis and may persist for months.9There is a small but potentially fatal risk of splenic rupture, estimated at 0.1%, up to 8 weeks after onset of infectious mononucleosis.10 The patient underwent a repeat rapid heterophile antibody test, which resulted in a positive monospot test result. The patient took ibuprofen and acetaminophen for the next week. Fourteen days later, all symptoms had completely resolved.

scenario: A 48-year-old woman with diet-controlled diabetes presented with a 6-month history of arthralgias in her hands, feet, elbows, and knees; 3 weeks of a purpuric rash and foot paresthesias; and 2 weeks of bilateral eye pain and redness. She had been prescribed 4 days of prednisone (10 mg/d) without improvement. She had no fevers, epistaxis, rhinorrhea, cough, shortness of breath, or hematuria. She had no history of recent travel or illicit drug use and was not taking any medications. On examination, her vital signs were normal. She had bilateral scleral injection and swelling and tenderness over the proximal interphalangeal joints bilaterally. Hemorrhagic vesicles and violaceous papules were present on her ears, nose, arms, and legs (Figure). Laboratory studies revealed normal complete blood cell count, serum electrolyte levels, and liver enzyme levels. Urinalysis findings were normal and urine toxicology screen was negative. Punch biopsy of a papule on the right arm demonstrated a superficial perivascular infiltrate of neutrophils with leukocytoclasia, extravasation of erythrocytes, and fibrin in small blood vessel walls. Direct immunofluorescence testing was negative for in situ deposits of IgG, IgA, IgM, and C3.

options.A: Check antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) titers
options.B: Check chikungunya serology
options.D: Order a urine nucleic acid amplification test for Chlamydia trachomatis

answer: Check antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) titers
distractors: Check chikungunya serology
Obtain a transthoracic echocardiogram
Order a urine nucleic acid amplification test for Chlamydia trachomatis
explanation: A. Check antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) titers The key to the correct diagnosis is the history of arthralgias, paresthesias, ocular inflammation, palpable purpura, and skin biopsy findings of leukocytoclasia, which is characteristic of small vessel vasculitis. ANCA-associated vasculitis due to granulomatosis with polyangiitis was confirmed with serum indirect immunofluorescence, diffuse cytoplasmic staining ANCA (c-ANCA) (+1:20), and a positive proteinase 3 (PR3) antibody (+51.8). Chikungunya (choice B) is a mosquito-borne viral illness that may cause arthralgias and conjunctivitis; however, its rash is morbilliform rather than purpuric. Obtaining a transthoracic echocardiogram (choice C) is incorrect because without fevers or history of intravenous drug use, endocarditis is unlikely. WhileChlamydia trachomatis(choice D) may cause a reactive arthritis with arthralgias and conjunctivitis, it does not cause cutaneous small vessel vasculitis. Vasculitides are diseases that involve inflammation of blood vessel walls. ANCA-associated vasculitis, a type of small vessel vasculitis, can affect any organ, including the skin, eyes, lungs, kidneys, joints, ears, nose, throat, and nervous system, and may cause constitutional symptoms, such as fatigue and weight loss.1ANCA-associated vasculitis includes granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly known as Wegener granulomatosis), microscopic polyangiitis, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly known as Churg-Strauss syndrome). Worldwide incidence of ANCA-associated vasculitis ranges from 13 to 20 cases per million per year2and peaks at age 60 to 70 years.3Cutaneous manifestations, including palpable purpura, petechiae, painful skin lesions, maculopapular rash, and splinter hemorrhages, are the presenting feature in 35% of patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis.4Patients with cutaneous manifestations are more likely to have severe systemic vasculitis than those without skin involvement.4 Diagnosis of ANCA-associated vasculitis is based on clinical features, pathology, and presence of ANCA, which are autoantibodies against specific proteins in neutrophils that can help delineate disease subtype.3There are 2 major ANCA indirect immunofluorescence patterns: c-ANCA, in which antibodies are typically directed against PR3, and p-ANCA, in which antibodies are typically directed against myeloperoxidase (MPO). ANCA serology should also be checked with a PR3/MPO enzyme-linked immunoassay to confirm the diagnosis of ANCA-associated vasculitis. On diagnosis of ANCA-associated vasculitis, the severity and extent of disease must be determined. Life-threatening disease includes alveolar hemorrhage, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, and severe cardiac, central nervous system, gastrointestinal, or ocular involvement.5In severe disease, induction therapy consists of pulse-dose glucocorticoids (typically 500-1000 mg/d for 1-3 days) combined with rituximab or cyclophosphamide. Patients are then typically treated with prednisone at a dose of 1 mg/kg per day, with a goal dose of 7.5 to 12.5 mg/d at 3 months.6For disease that is not severe, induction therapy typically includes oral prednisone at a dose of 0.5 mg/kg per day for 2 to 4 weeks, along with methotrexate or mycophenolate mofetil.5For maintenance of remission, rituximab is currently preferred.5However, methotrexate, azathioprine, leflunomide, and mycophenolate mofetil may be used if rituximab is contraindicated or unavailable.7 Before identification of high-dose glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide as effective treatments, the mortality rate attributable to ANCA-associated vasculitis was up to 80% within 1 year of diagnosis.8With current treatments, 5-year survival rates are 74% to 91% for granulomatosis with polyangiitis and 45% to 76% for microscopic polyangiitis.9However, patients must be carefully monitored for relapses, which may result in severe organ damage (eg, end-stage kidney disease). Additionally, patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis may experience complications from treatment with immunosuppressive medications, including infections, hypertension, diabetes, weight gain, malignancy, and osteoporosis.3 A complete workup demonstrated no evidence of kidney or pulmonary involvement. For induction therapy, the patient received intravenous pulse-dose methylprednisolone and 2 doses of intravenous rituximab 2 weeks apart. She was transitioned to an oral prednisone taper with a plan to continue intravenous rituximab every 6 months. Her symptoms improved, and she remained asymptomatic apart from fading papules on the thighs while receiving prednisone (20 mg daily) at her last visit 6 months later.

scenario: A 69-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of progressive skin discoloration. His medical history included chronic kidney disease, chronic hepatitis C infection, cirrhosis, ischemic cardiomyopathy with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), and atrial fibrillation with prophylactic apixaban. He had recurrent staphylococcus bacteremia due to infection of an ICD lead and had been treated for the past 6 months with minocycline, 100 mg twice daily. His arms had been purple and bruise-like for several years but turned a near black color 1 month ago. He reported no discoloration of his sweat or urine. He had no history of malnutrition and reported infrequent alcohol use. Physical examination showed dense blue-black skin pigmentation of his forearms, dorsal hands, legs, and dorsal feet, as well as blue discoloration of his sclerae and teeth (Figure 1). He had normal-colored nails and oral mucosa. Laboratory studies showed white blood cell count of 15 800/μL (reference range, 4000-11 000/μL), hemoglobin of 10.7 g/dL (reference, 13.5-17.5 g/dL), platelet count of 58 000/μL (reference, 150 000-400 000/μL), and INR of 1.8 (reference, 0.8-1.1). Complete metabolic panel showed increased creatinine (1.51 mg/dL; reference, 0.64-1.27 mg/dL) and elevated total bilirubin (1.7 mg/dL; reference range, 0.3-1.2 mg/dL). His estimated glomerular filtration rate was 40 mL/min/1.73 m2.

options.A: Discontinue apixaban
options.B: Discontinue minocycline

answer: Discontinue minocycline
distractors: Discontinue apixaban
Order serum iron studies
Order serum niacin levels
explanation: The keys to the correct diagnosis are the blue-black color of the pigmentation, the location on the distal extremities, and the involvement of sclerae and teeth. Potential etiologies for blue skin discoloration include drug-induced (eg, amiodarone, minocycline, hydroxychloroquine, and fluoroquinolones1), exposure to silver (argyria) or gold salts (chrysiasis), and deposition of pigmented fibers due to an inherited enzyme deficiency (endogenous ochronosis or alkaptonuria) or hydroquinone use (exogenous ochronosis).2Given this patient’s ongoing minocycline use, discontinuing minocycline is the best answer. This patient’s ecchymoses, most prominent at his proximal forearms, represent a distinct process from the blue-black pigmentation caused by minocycline. The ecchymoses were due to his use of apixaban, thrombocytopenia, bleeding diathesis, and skin fragility from age and sun exposure and would not necessitate stopping apixaban (choice A). Hemochromatosis (choice C) causes skin dyspigmentation that is typically diffuse and brown or slate-gray.3Pellagra, caused by deficiency in niacin (vitamin B3) (choice D), presents with a photodistributed rash; however, the rash is red or brown and does not discolor sclerae or teeth.2 Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation presents as blue-hued pigmentation of the skin that may also involve the sclerae, nails, teeth, and oral mucosa. The reported incidence varies from 2% to 15% in patients treated for acne to 41% to 54% in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and orthopedic infections, respectively.4-6 Although minocycline-induced cutaneous hyperpigmentation is a clinical diagnosis, skin biopsy can confirm the diagnosis and reveals subepidermal deposition of granular black pigment both interstitially and intracellularly (Figure 2). The pigment reacts positively with staining techniques used to detect iron and/or melanin (Perl’s Prussian blue and Fontana-Masson, respectively). In contrast, ecchymoses stain positive for iron only. While the mechanism of hyperpigmentation remains unclear, histopathologic studies indicate that minocycline and/or its metabolites likely form insoluble complexes with iron that deposit in tissue.7 Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation is classified into 3 types based on clinical findings and histologic staining, though these categories may overlap. In type I, blue pigmentation is found in scars, commonly facial acne scars, and stains positive for iron only. In type II, blue pigmentation affects normal skin, typically on the extremities, and stains positive for both iron and melanin. Type III presents with muddy brown discoloration most prominent in sun-exposed skin and stains positive for melanin.8 This patient’s presentation was consistent with type II hyperpigmentation and notable for both the striking degree of pigmentation and for its rapid development after only 6 months of treatment. Most minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation occurs after a year, though small case series have reported pigmentation after only a few weeks.5,6,9Several characteristics of this patient may have contributed to the more rapid onset, including the longstanding purpura on his arms, which increases dermal iron available for chelation, as well as hepatic and kidney disease, which impair drug metabolism and excretion. Minocycline-induced cutaneous hyperpigmentation persists after drug cessation and is challenging to treat. Given the small size of the pigment particle, treatment is best approached with picosecond or Q-switched lasers.10In addition to its effects on skin pigmentation, minocycline use in children can result in permanent teeth discoloration and bone hypoplasia and should be avoided during pregnancy and in children younger than 8 years old.2 Minocycline was discontinued and daptomycin was started in its place. The patient declined treatment for the pigmentation changes because they were not bothersome to him.

scenario: A 42-year-old woman was referred for ophthalmologic evaluation after developing blurry vision in the right eye 30 days prior. She had a history of hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and migraine headaches. Her medications included atorvastatin, carvedilol, and norethindrone. Dilated-fundus examination of the right eye showed a single cotton-wool spot (indicating local retinal ischemia), with intraretinal hemorrhage in the inferotemporal quadrant. Ultrawide-field imaging showed a cotton-wool spot on the left fundus (Figure 1A, right) and a peripheral arterial occlusion in the right eye (Figure 1A, left), and fluorescein angiographic study of the right eye demonstrated an area of blockage corresponding to intraretinal hemorrhage and venous hyperfluorescence (Figure 1B). The patient was afebrile, with pulse 110 beats/min and blood pressure of 188/99 mm Hg. Auscultation over the heart apex revealed a holosystolic ejection murmur (grade 2/6). Laboratory testing showed normal complete blood cell count and thyrotropin level and negative results for autoantibodies against Sm, SSA, SSB, Scl-70, Jo-1, centromere, chromatin, ribonucleoprotein, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was mildly elevated (30 mm/h). Results of testing for antinuclear antibodies were positive at low titer (1:40, homogenous pattern) with positive dsDNA (5.0 IU/mL; negative if <4.0 IU/mL). Blood cultures were negative for bacterial or fungal growth after 5 days. An echocardiogram revealed pedunculated and mobile aortic valve vegetations.

options.A: Administer intravenous antibiotics
options.B: Administer systemic corticosteroids

answer: Check antiphospholipid antibody levels
distractors: Administer intravenous antibiotics
Administer systemic corticosteroids
Administer anticoagulant therapy
explanation: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE) associated with primary antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) D. Check antiphospholipid antibody levels The key to the correct diagnosis was the presence of systemic features of a prothrombotic state and endothelial injury involving more than 1 anatomical site (ie, retinal artery thrombosis and aortic valve findings). Although a cotton-wool spot with surrounding hemorrhage (Roth spot) has been classically associated with bacterial endocarditis, it is a nonspecific finding and has also been associated with APS, autoimmune disease, hematologic malignancy, diabetic retinopathy, preeclampsia, and shaken baby syndrome. Intravenous antibiotics for infectious endocarditis (choice A) would not be appropriate in the absence of fevers, markedly elevated inflammatory marker levels, or abnormal blood cultures. While a prothrombotic state may be associated with autoimmune disease, empirical treatment with systemic corticosteroids (choice B) or anticoagulation (choice C) should not be initiated without additional workup, including antiphospholipid antibody testing (choice D). APS is an autoimmune disease characterized by a prothrombotic/procoagulant state with clinical evidence of vascular thrombosis and laboratory evidence of elevated levels of antiphospholipid antibodies measured at least 12 weeks apart. APS may be classified as either a primary disease or secondary in the setting of another autoimmune disease (ie, systemic lupus erythematosus).1,2Primary and secondary APS typically present in the fourth decade of life, with prevalence increasing with age, and risk factors include smoking, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypertension. NBTE is a form of endothelial injury affecting the endothelial lined surfaces of the heart, particularly the valves.3NBTE has been associated with autoimmune diseases (including APS), prothrombotic states, exposure to toxins (including chemotherapeutic agents), malignancy, and physical injury.4 Evaluation for NBTE should include testing for APS (via antiphospholipid antibodies), autoimmune disease, and additional prothrombotic states. Testing for antiphospholipid antibodies includes anticardiolipin or anti-β2-glycoprotein 1 antibodies (IgG and IgM) or lupus anticoagulant. Testing for systemic autoimmune disease includes antinuclear antibodies, DNA, anti-Sm, and Scl-70. Testing for other prothrombotic states should include assays for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (specifically forADAMTS13variants), coagulation factor abnormalities (eg, factor V Leiden variants, prothrombin variants, plasminogen, thrombomodulin), as well as pathways involved in atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome  (eg, factor H, factor I, complement gene variants). This patient met criteria for APS based on evidence of vascular thrombosis and endothelial injury as well as elevated levels of antiphospholipid antibodies (specifically, positive result for lupus anticoagulant testing and elevated levels of anticardiolipin antibodies IgG and IgM); she did not meet criteria for a diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus or any other autoimmune disease.1,5 Approximately one-third of patients with primary APS have echocardiographic evidence of cardiac valvular abnormalities such as thickening or vegetations.6Prevalence of ocular involvement with vaso-occlusive disease in patients with primary APS ranges from 22% to 29%.7,8Ocular findings may represent either sequelae of localized APS-mediated endothelial injury and subsequent thrombosis or a thromboembolism due to the valvular-derived APS-mediated vegetations. Low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg/d) is suggested as primary thromboprophylaxis in patients with APS.2For secondary thromboprophylaxis after either an arterial or venous thrombotic event, oral anticoagulation therapy with warfarin combined with low-dose aspirin is recommended indefinitely.2Patients with NBTE may be considered for valvular surgery (valve replacement or excision of the vegetation) when there is severe valvular regurgitation, the vegetation is larger than 2 cm, or in the setting of thromboembolic events related to valvular vegetation.9 Antiphospholipid testing showed positive lupus anticoagulant (dilute Russell viper venom test ratio, 2.02 [negative if <1.20]; silica clotting time test ratio, 2.88 [negative if <1.16]) and elevated anticardiolipin antibodies IgG and IgM levels (both >40 U/mL; positive if >40 U/mL). The patient underwent aortic valve and aortic root replacement without complication. Cultures from the valve vegetations were negative for bacterial or fungal growth. Vegetations stained positive for fibrin, consistent with NBTE (Figure 2). The patient was prescribed anticoagulation with warfarin (target international normalized ratio, 3.0) and has not had new clinical complications or manifestations of APS 4 months postoperatively.

scenario: A 47-year-old man with melanoma and a history of papillary thyroid cancer treated with thyroidectomy presented with 1 week of low-grade fevers, myalgias, and proximal muscle weakness. Three months earlier, he underwent digital amputation of his right third finger and began adjuvant nivolumab treatment for stage IIIC acral-lentiginous melanoma. One week later, he developed fevers, myalgias, dark urine, weakness, and difficulty walking. He had no palpitations, chest pain, or shortness of breath. On examination, his blood pressure was 135/86 mm Hg, pulse 78/min, and he was afebrile. He had reduced strength in bilateral proximal shoulders (3/5), elbow flexors/extensors (3/5), and forearm flexors/extensors (4+/5). No rashes were noted. Laboratory studies demonstrated a creatine kinase (CK) level of 111 859 U/L (reference range, 30-220 U/L), CK-MB of 270 ng/mL (reference, <8 ng/mL), and aldolase above 500 U/L (reference, <7.7 U/L). Aspartate aminotransferase level was 1980 U/L (reference range, 15-41 U/L), alanine aminotransferase was 814 U/L (reference range, 14-54 U/L), creatinine was 4.9 mg/dL (reference range, 0.4-1.0 mg/dL) with a previously normal baseline, and potassium was 6.4 mmol/L (reference range, 3.5-5.0 mmol/L). Urinalysis showed 27 red blood cells (reference range, 0-5) and myoglobin above 5000 µg/L (reference, 0 µg/L). Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 67 mm/h (reference, <20 mm/h) and C-reactive protein was 10.2 mg/dL (reference, ≤0.60 mg/dL). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the left humerus demonstrated T2 flare most pronounced within the biceps and anterior lateral deltoid muscles (Figure). The patient’s electrocardiogram (ECG) is also shown in theFigure.

options.A: Start intravenous immune globulin
options.B: Measure troponin and natriuretic peptides, and perform an echocardiogram

answer: Measure troponin and natriuretic peptides, and perform an echocardiogram
distractors: Start intravenous immune globulin
Start intravenous fluids
Obtain muscle biopsy
explanation: B. Measure troponin and natriuretic peptides, and perform an echocardiogram The key to the correct diagnosis was the presence of muscle weakness, elevated CK, and MRI changes consistent with myositis, occurring after nivolumab administration. Nivolumab-associated myositis may be associated with myocarditis, which can be asymptomatic. The ECG showed ST-segment elevations in the anterior (V1-V3) and anterolateral (V4-V6) leads with PR depressions in lead II and V4-V6, consistent with myopericarditis-type changes. Intravenous immune globulin (IVIG) is an effective treatment for  myositis associated with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy and IV fluids would treat rhabdomyolysis, but both could cause volume overload and acute heart failure without first evaluating left ventricular function. While muscle biopsy would definitively diagnose myositis, this is not the most appropriate next step due to its invasive nature. Immune checkpoint inhibitors are monoclonal antibodies that treat malignancies including melanoma, lung cancer, urothelial carcinoma, and lymphoma. Immune checkpoint inhibitors can cause immune-related adverse events affecting the skin (7%-34% treated patients reporting), gastrointestinal tract (7%-50%), and endocrine system (8%-23%).1,2Rarely, rheumatic and cardiac manifestations may occur.2 Rheumatic immune-related adverse events include inflammatory arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica–like syndrome, sicca syndrome, and myositis.3The incidence of myositis is approximately 0.15% (27/17 620) for nivolumab monotherapy and 0.24% (7/2974) for combination therapy with nivolumab and ipilimumab.4Cardiac involvement, including myocarditis and pericarditis, occurs in approximately 16% of patients with immune checkpoint inhibitor–associated myositis.5,6Myositis may occur sooner after administration than other rheumatic immune-related adverse events, often within weeks.5,7Though uncommon, myositis with immune checkpoint inhibitor–associated myocarditis has an approximate 50% mortality rate.5Some patients, as in this case, are asymptomatic, and thus cardiac screening may be useful. However, no randomized clinical trials have demonstrated that using echocardiography to screen for myocarditis in this setting improves outcomes. Prior studies have shown that elevated troponin and abnormal ECG findings were present in 94% and 89%, respectively, of immune checkpoint inhibitor–associated myocarditis cases, even when left ventricular ejection fraction remained normal.8Elevated troponin, natriuretic peptide levels, and echocardiographic longitudinal strain impairment were associated with adverse cardiac events, including cardiovascular death, cardiogenic shock, cardiac arrest, and complete heart block.8Late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI has low sensitivity (48%) for diagnosis of immune checkpoint inhibitor–associated myocarditis.9Endomyocardial biopsy may be pursued when clinical suspicion persists after nondiagnostic noninvasive testing.4 The American Society of Clinical Oncology guidelines for immune-related adverse event treatment for grade 4 myositis (weakness limiting self-care activities) are as follows: (1) hold the checkpoint inhibitor, (2) administer high-dose steroids (prednisone, 0.5-2 mg/kg/d or methylprednisolone, 1000 mg IV daily bolus for 3-5 days if severe compromise [weakness severely limiting mobility, cardiac, respiratory, dysphagia]), (3) consider IVIG, and (4) consider other immunosuppressants in 4 to 6 weeks if symptoms persist (such as methotrexate, azathioprine, or mycophenolate mofetil).10For myocarditis, recommendations based on expert opinion include medical therapy for heart failure, cardiac rhythm monitoring, and consideration of antiarrhythmic treatment, given the potential for conduction disease and arrhythmic events.4 The patient had N-terminal pro–brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) of 2238 pg/mL (reference,  ≤125 pg/mL) and high-sensitivity troponin of 1545 ng/L. Echocardiogram demonstrated normal left ventricular ejection fraction (>55%) without valvular abnormalities or pericardial effusion. Antinuclear antibody was positive with 1:160 speckled pattern, negative extractable nuclear antigen, negative double-stranded DNA, and negative myositis autoantibody panel. Muscle biopsy demonstrated necrotizing myopathy, confirming a diagnosis of immune checkpoint inhibitor–associated myositis. He was treated with 1000 mg of IV methylprednisolone for 3 days followed by oral prednisone, and his myositis resolved with normalization of CK and CK-MB. He required temporary hemodialysis, but had full kidney recovery. Two years after initial presentation, he continues to have normal kidney function and his myositis remains in remission.

caption: Patchy, nonpruritic hair loss on the scalp of a 36-year-old man
scenario: A 36-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 3 weeks of generalized weakness and a dry cough. He reported hair loss for 1 month. Medical history was significant for opioid and alcohol use disorders, injection drug use, and chronic HIV infection. He discontinued his antiretroviral therapy 2 years prior to presentation. At that time, his CD4+cell count was 820/μL and his HIV viral load was undetectable. On presentation, his heart rate was 88/min and regular; blood pressure, 90/58 mm Hg; oxygen saturation, 100% on room air; and respiratory rate, 20/min. He was afebrile. Cardiorespiratory auscultation was deferred because a diagnosis of COVID-19 was considered. He had a faint maculopapular rash on his arms and torso and patchy hair loss on his scalp (Figure). There were no genital lesions or mucosal ulcerations. Laboratory testing revealed a hemoglobin level of 9.5 g/dL, white blood cell count of 7500/μL, and platelet count of 152 ×103/μL. Chest radiography demonstrated consolidation in the right lower lobe. A nasopharyngeal swab for SARS-CoV-2 was negative. He was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone.

options.B: Check rapid plasma reagin (RPR) level

distractors: Check antinuclear antibody level
Obtain skin scrapings of the scalp
Perform punch biopsy of the scalp
explanation: “Moth-eaten” alopecia caused by secondary syphilis B. Check rapid plasma reagin (RPR) level The key to the correct diagnosis was the “moth-eaten” pattern of hair loss associated with a faint maculopapular rash. These findings in the setting of chronic HIV infection suggested a diagnosis of secondary syphilis. This patient did not have other features of systemic lupus erythematosus, such as a malar rash, photosensitivity, or mouth ulcerations, to support ordering an antinuclear antibody screen (choice A). Examination of skin scrapings (choice C) can diagnose tinea capitis, but tinea capitis was unlikely because the alopecia was noninflammatory based on lack of scaling or perifollicular erythema. Punch biopsy of the scalp (choice D) can diagnose alopecia areata and may demonstrate the characteristic perivascular plasmacytic infiltration of syphilis, but biopsy was considered invasive prior to performing serologic testing for syphilis. Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection cause by the spirocheteTreponema pallidum.1-3Syphilis is transmitted when an infectious lesion contacts the skin or mucous membranes of an uninfected person. It can also be transmitted through bloodborne means or by vertical transmission during pregnancy and childbirth.1-3Since 2000, there has been a dramatic increase in the rates of primary and secondary syphilis in the US.1,4In 2019, the incidence of secondary syphilis was 11.9 cases per 100 000 population.5In men, the incidence was 20.1 per 100 000 population.5Men who have sex with men accounted for 47.1% of all cases.6Approximately 44% of men diagnosed with primary and secondary syphilis are HIV-positive.7In 2019, the incidence of primary and secondary syphilis in women increased to 3.9 per 100 000 population5and the incidence of congenital syphilis increased to 48.3 cases per 100 000 live births.5 Primary syphilis is characterized by a painless, clean-based infectious lesion, a chancre, at the site of inoculation.1,3,8The mean incubation period is approximately 21 days (range, 10-90 days).3The chancre heals with or without treatment in approximately 3 to 6 weeks. Secondary syphilis occurs from hematogenous dissemination of spirochetes at the time of the initial infection and has varied clinical manifestations. Secondary syphilis typically occurs 3 to 12 weeks after the primary infection.1Signs may include a cutaneous exanthem (eg, palmoplantar rash), mucous patches and condylomata lata (moist, highly infectious flat-topped papules in intertriginous areas in the groin), lymphadenopathy, and constitutional symptoms including malaise, myalgias, and low-grade fever.1,3,8Hair and nail changes occur less frequently. Syphilitic alopecia is noninflammatory and nonscarring and is associated with secondary syphilis.1,9It presents in a diffuse pattern, a patchy “moth-eaten” pattern, or a combination.9Alopecia in secondary syphilis is attributed to an immune response to spirochetal antigens in hair follicles.10Alopecia is a relatively uncommon presentation of syphilis (4%-12% of cases of secondary syphilis) and can mimic alopecia areata both clinically and histopathologically.1Current guidelines recommend a single intramuscular dose of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin G for treatment of both primary and secondary syphilis; tertiary syphilis should be treated with aqueous penicillin G, 3 to 4 million units intravenously every 4 hours, for 10 to 14 days.2Alopecia due to syphilis resolves with treatment. Blood cultures obtained on admission grew penicillin-sensitiveStreptococcus pneumoniae. After discharge, the patient’s RPR titer was 1:2048, with a positive treponemal-specific confirmatory test result (Treponema pallidumparticle agglutination), confirming a diagnosis of secondary syphilis. Based on strong clinical suspicion for secondary syphilis, the patient received a single intramuscular dose of 2.4 million units of penicillin G prior to discharge (in addition to antibiotic therapy for pneumococcal disease).2His previous antiretroviral therapy was restarted, and he was prescribed buprenorphine/naloxone for his opioid use disorder. After discharge, his HIV viral load was 46 774 copies/mL. Multiple attempts to reach the patient to schedule a lumbar puncture to exclude a diagnosis of asymptomatic neurosyphilis were initially unsuccessful. However, 6 months after discharge, the patient requested to reengage in care and reported hair regrowth.

scenario: A 71-year-old woman with a history of intermittent generalized pruritus of unclear etiology and right knee osteoarthritis underwent total knee arthroplasty. She presented 8 weeks postoperatively with a 1-week history of scattered pruritic bullae around her incision site. She reported that the symptoms were unlike any rashes she had had before. She had no fever, knee pain, or lower extremity swelling. She was taking no medications and had no allergies. On examination, she was afebrile and well-appearing. Knee examination showed no effusion and normal range of motion without pain. Her incision was fully healed. Several 1- to 2-cm tense, fluid-filled bullae were present around the incision. There was no surrounding erythema or edema. She received topical iodine for 2 weeks, during which time 4 new tense bullae appeared (Figure, left panel). Three bullae subsequently ruptured, while 1 remained intact. Drainage from the ruptured bullae was clear. She was advised to continue using iodine on the affected skin for wound care and was prescribed a 7-day course of oral cephalexin and a tapering regimen of low-dose prednisone. After completion of the antibiotic course, the bullae and pruritus remained unchanged (Figure, right panel). Superficial cultures of the bullae were negative for bacterial growth.

options.B: Perform skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence study

answer: Perform skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence study
distractors: Aspirate the knee for synovial cell count with differential, culture, Gram stain, and examination for crystals
Perform skin patch testing
Order trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, 160/80 mg twice daily for 7 days
explanation: B. Perform skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence study The key to the correct diagnosis was the pattern of tense bullae with clear exudate and associated severe pruritus, typical for bullous pemphigoid. Recognizing bullous pemphigoid features helps avoid unnecessary antimicrobial treatment and diagnostic interventions. Biopsy with direct immunofluorescence (DIF) revealed a linear pattern of IgG along the dermal-epidermal junction, consistent with the diagnosis of bullous pemphigoid.1Aspiration of the knee to investigate for prosthetic joint infection (choice A) is not indicated in this case, as the patient had no symptoms concerning for an intra-articular infection, such as pain or warmth. A diagnosis of allergic and irritant contact dermatitis (ACD) may be confirmed with skin patch testing (choice C); however, in this patient, the bullae were larger than would be expected for ACD, and symptoms would have appeared earlier in the postoperative course and should have resolved with oral corticosteroids. Further antibiotic treatment for bullous impetigo (choice D) would not be indicated for this patient, as the clinical appearance was not consistent with impetigo (lack of honey-crusted lesions) and there was no improvement with either topical iodine or oral cephalexin. Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune blistering disorder characterized by the presence of IgG autoantibodies directed against hemidesmosomes in the dermal-epidermal junction. As in this patient, bullous pemphigoid most commonly occurs in patients older than 70 years. Bullous pemphigoid is usually a generalized, widespread and chronic autoimmune condition favoring flexural skin surfaces. Bullous pemphigoid arising after surgery is rare but has been described; therefore, clinicians should be aware of bullous pemphigoid as a possible cause of postoperative wound complications involving bullae.2-5Drug-induced bullous pemphigoid is also possible; common medications that can cause bullous pemphigoid include gliptins, diuretics such as furosemide, antibiotics including amoxicillin and ciprofloxacin, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors such as lisinopril. Clinical presentation consists of tense, polymorphic, fluid-containing bullae larger than 1 cm in diameter. Bullae may develop on either erythematous or normal-appearing skin and are often associated with severe pruritus.6,7The bullae have a negative Nikolsky sign (no separation of epidermis on manual shearing force). The differential diagnosis for this patient included ACD, bullous impetigo, and pemphigus vulgaris. ACD results from a hypersensitivity reaction to an allergen, with a more rapid onset with previous sensitization.8Surgical settings involve a wide range of potential allergens including tapes, sutures, glues, and dressings. ACD usually presents as an erythematous pruritic rash that may include superficial vesicles or bullae and usually occurs 7 to 10 days after initial allergen exposure or within 12 to 48 hours after reexposure.8 Bullous pemphigoid and bullous impetigo can appear similar, but bullous impetigo has an infectious etiology. Bullous impetigo tends to occur in younger children and presents with flaccid blisters that rupture easily and leave a collarette of scale and honey-colored crust. Pemphigus vulgaris is a potentially fatal blistering skin disorder to be considered in the differential. It differs from bullous pemphigoid in that it has a positive Nikolsky sign, oral mucosa involvement, and DIF pattern of IgG antibodies against desmoglein, which reveals antibodies around epidermal cells in a reticular pattern. Skin biopsy and DIF is considered the gold standard for the diagnosis of bullous pemphigoid.1Biopsy shows subepidermal bulla containing numerous eosinophils, and DIF demonstrates a linear deposition of IgG, C3, or both along the basement membrane as well as separation along the dermal-epidermal junction.7,9Other studies include serum enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay to detect the main autoantigens BP180 and BP230.6 For mild disease, superpotent topical corticosteroids, such as clobetasol or halobetasol, are used for treatment of bullous pemphigoid.10Antibiotics with anti-inflammatory properties, such as doxycycline, can also be used, although the mechanism of action is not well understood. For moderate to severe disease, systemic corticosteroid therapy is the treatment of choice. Adjunctive therapy includes methotrexate, dapsone, and mycophenolate mofetil. The patient was treated with topical halobetasol on an intermittent basis for 7 to 10 days at a time, whereupon she would develop new blisters. Her pruritus and bullae ultimately resolved after several months. She had no further complications from her total knee arthroplasty.

scenario: An 82-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 2 months of diarrhea and 2 weeks of rash. She had sustained a left radius fracture 6 months prior, which resulted in deconditioning and poor appetite. Her diet consisted of mostly vegetables, and she lost 4 kg (8.8 lb) during this time. Two months prior, she developed postprandial nonbloody diarrhea that occurred 5 times daily. Two weeks prior, a pruritic rash in her extremities emerged. She had no fever, night sweats, or abdominal pain. Past medical history included chronic nondeforming rheumatoid arthritis, hypothyroidism, and colon adenocarcinoma resected 10 years prior. Her medications were prednisolone (1 mg/d) and levothyroxine. On examination, she was afebrile, with blood pressure 90/46 mm Hg; pulse, 90/min and regular; and respirations, 18/min. Body mass index was 16.8 (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared). She was alert, cognitively intact, and appeared emaciated. Glossitis and a scaly pruritic rash with an erythematous brawny peeling base on her neck and extremities were noted (Figure). Findings on cardiovascular, pulmonary, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed mild hyponatremia (132 mmol/L) and an otherwise normal basic metabolic panel. Other laboratory values were as follows: C-reactive protein, 0.58 mg/dL; erythrocyte sedimentation rate, 23 mm/h; total protein, 4.8 g/dL; and albumin, 1.8 g/dL. Her white blood cell count was 7200/μL (66.5% neutrophils, 30.4% lymphocytes); hemoglobin level, 9.9 g/dL; mean corpuscular volume, 96 fL; and platelet count, 332 000/μL. Results of liver function tests, coagulation tests, urinalysis, thyroid function tests, measurement of serum vitamin B12and folic acid levels, and cosyntropin stimulation tests were normal. Serum copper level was 46 μg (reference range, 66-130 μg) and zinc level was 23 μg (reference, ≥80 μg). Abdominal computed tomography revealed no abnormalities.

explanation: C. Measure serum niacin level The key to the correct diagnosis in this patient is the presence of persistent nonbloody diarrhea, rash in sun-exposed areas, and glossitis in an older frail woman with severe malnutrition—features key to diagnosing pellagra, which is characterized by 4 Ds (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, and death) if left untreated.1 Measurement of fecal calprotectin level (choice A) is not indicated in this patient with no findings of inflammatory bowel disease such as fever, abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, or elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Because skin changes in sun-exposed areas and glossitis are atypical of parasitic infection and this patient had no eosinophilia, checking for fecal ova and parasites (choice B) also is not indicated. Given the patient’s symptoms suggestive of pellagra, measurement of serum niacin level (choice C) would be appropriate. Testing for serum antitissue transglutaminase antibody (choice D), a screening test for celiac disease, is not immediately indicated in this patient, as her rash is not consistent with dermatitis herpetiformis. Pellagra is the result of dietary deficiency or malabsorption of niacin (vitamin B3), also known as nicotinic acid and nicotinamide, or its precursor, tryptophan. Dietary sources of niacin include fish, meat, nuts, eggs, and nutrient-fortified foods, such as cereal and bread.2Niacin is a water-soluble vitamin and a precursor of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate, which are important coenzymes of cellular metabolism of macronutrients such as carbohydrate, protein, and fat.3Niacin is rapidly absorbed from the stomach and small intestine. Deficiency of niacin affects organs with high energy requirements or high turnover rates, such as the brain, skin, and gut.2 Pellagra is uncommon in developed countries4; a study from Spain reported an annual incidence of 0.5 cases per 100 000 population.5A high index of suspicion aids diagnosis and treatment of this fatal but curable disease.1Conditions associated with pellagra include malnutrition (anorexia nervosa, malignancy, or HIV infection), gastrointestinal malabsorption (Crohn disease), alcohol misuse, hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis, use of certain drugs (isoniazid or azathioprine), and carcinoid syndrome.1,6In this case, prolonged anorexia and dietary restriction to only vegetables led to niacin deficiency. Pellagra is characterized by dermatologic, gastrointestinal, and neuropsychiatric symptoms. Skin manifestations develop bilaterally and symmetrically in sun-exposed areas. The skin manifestation starts as erythema and itching and subsequently becomes edematous. Thickening, dryness, roughness, hyperpigmentation, and eruption with desquamation may also occur.7Gastrointestinal features develop in approximately half of patients with pellagra and include glossitis, stomatitis, and intractable diarrhea due to the atrophy of gastrointestinal mucosa.2,4Neuropsychiatric symptoms are present in 40% of patients, developing late in the course.8The most common neurologic manifestation is impaired cognitive functioning, but hallucinations, thought disturbances, anxiety, depression, and parkinsonism may also be seen. Pellagra is treated with nicotinamide (300 mg/d in divided doses) for several weeks or until resolution of symptoms, along with a high-protein diet, other B vitamins, and trace elements such as zinc.2,4Clinical symptoms usually improve within a few days of treatment. After the patient was hospitalized her prednisolone dosage was increased to 5 mg/d to prevent adrenal insufficiency. Stool studies did not reveal any organisms. Colonoscopy and random biopsy of the colon demonstrated no findings of inflammation, malignancy, or amyloidosis. Pellagra was suspected, and vitamins including niacin and trace elements were supplemented. However, she developed methicillin-resistantStaphylococcus aureussepsis, resulting from superinfection of her rash, and died on hospital day 17. A previous niacin level was low, at 3.8 μg/mL (reference range, 4.7-7.9).

scenario: A 28-year-old man presented to his primary care physician for hematochezia. He had previously lived for a few years in Uganda and frequently swam in the Nile River. After returning to the US, he experienced recurrent diarrhea. In April 2018, he had an appendectomy for acute appendicitis. In February 2019, 22 months after his return from Uganda, he developed intermittent hematochezia. He had no vomiting, fever, or weight loss during this time. On evaluation, vital signs were normal and abdominal examination showed a soft, nontender abdomen. Rectal examination was normal. A complete blood cell count and comprehensive metabolic panel were notable for a normal hemoglobin level and an absolute eosinophil count of 304 cells/μL. Results of testing including stool microscopy, HIV fourth-generation assay, hepatitis B serologies, and a rectal swab for gonorrhea and chlamydia were negative. A colonoscopy demonstrated granular mucosa in the rectum. Internal hemorrhoids were present, but there were no masses, vascular malformations, or other abnormalities. A biopsy of rectal tissue was obtained; histopathologic features are shown in theFigure.

options.B: Send 2 additional stool samples for ova and parasite detection

distractors: Send 2 additional stool samples for ova and parasite detection

explanation: A. Prescribe praziquantel without further diagnostic testing The key to the correct diagnosis in this patient is the histopathologic finding of granulomas containing schistosome eggs (Figure, black arrows) with lateral spines (Figure, blue arrow), consistent withSchistosoma mansoni,for which praziquantel is indicated (choice A). Although stool microscopy (choice B) is an appropriate first step, returning travelers often have low parasite burdens, so additional stool samples are low yield. The presence of schistosome eggs argues against tuberculosis as the cause of the granulomatous inflammation, so tuberculosis testing (choice C) and treatment (choice D) are not warranted. Schistosomiasis is a parasitic infection caused by flukes.Schistosoma mansoni,found in Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, resides in mesenteric venules, leading to intestinal, hepatic, and/or pulmonary disease as a result of an immune response to migrating eggs that deposit in these organs.1Infection is acquired through freshwater contact, from which larvae infect humans via skin penetration.2Exposure to upper Nile River water is a risk factor forS mansoniacquisition. In one study, 17% of persons exposed to Ugandan Nile River water developed acute schistosomiasis.3 Chronic schistosomiasis, more common in individuals with repeated exposures, is characterized by granulomatous inflammation that can progress to tissue fibrosis.4﻿Schistosoma mansonieggs deposit in the intestinal wall, liver, and lungs. Intestinal disease often presents as diarrhea, which can be bloody, and can also lead to acute appendicitis.4In a series of 304 cases of surgically treated appendicitis from South Africa, 10% had histopathologic evidence of schistosomiasis.5This patient’s appendix pathology specimen was negative for schistosomiasis on retrospective review. Advanced colonic disease can lead to intestinal stenosis or protein-losing enteropathy. Hepatic involvement leads to hepatosplenomegaly and abdominal pain.1Chronic hepatic infection can lead to periportal fibrosis, portal hypertension, variceal bleeding, and ascites4; lung involvement may lead to pulmonary hypertension. Schistosomiasis may not be on the differential diagnosis for rectal bleeding for physicians in nonendemic areas. Examination of stool for eggs is an appropriate first step, but this approach has limitations.6Eggs are not shed in excreta until 2 months after initial infection and shedding varies over time, affecting the yield of stool microscopy.1The negative predictive value of a single specimen is low in endemic areas.7When disease prevalence (>20%) or clinical suspicion is high, diagnostic yield increases with examination of multiple samples.7The diagnosis can still be missed, especially in returning travelers, in whom the parasite burden is usually low.6In a study of travelers returning to the UK, microscopy detected only 45% of cases.8A colonic biopsy is often diagnostic and indicated when the diagnosis is uncertain or when suspicion for schistosomiasis is high despite negative microscopy.1,2Serology cannot reliably distinguish between active and prior infection, as antibodies can persist for years after infection. However, serology may be useful to diagnose returning travelers for whom other testing is negative because of low parasite burdens.4,6 HumanSchistosomaspecies are universally susceptible to praziquantel, which is the treatment of choice. Praziquantel is inactive against immature worms, so returning travelers should receive treatment 6 to 8 weeks after their last exposure to contaminated water to allow for worm maturation; otherwise, a repeat course of treatment may be required.2,6,9MostS mansoniinfections can be treated with a 1-day course of praziquantel, given in 2 divided doses. In the event of persistent symptoms or eosinophilia after treatment, a second course of treatment is indicated.1When microscopy is positive for ova, it should be repeated 1 to 2 months after treatment to ensure eradication. If ova are again seen, another course of therapy is indicated.6,9 The patient was treated with praziquantel for 1 day, with symptom resolution. He was followed up for 1 year after treatment, and his hematochezia did not recur.

scenario: A 48-year-old man with a history of gastroesophageal reflux disease and obstructive sleep apnea presented with a rash over his right foot accompanied by 1 week of episodic fever, diaphoresis, and headaches. Six weeks prior, he fell from a ladder and had right nondisplaced medial malleolar and comminuted talar fractures. The fractures were managed nonsurgically in a controlled ankle movement boot, with resolution of swelling and bruising. On current presentation, his temperature was 38.2 °C (100.8 °F); heart rate, 88/min; respiratory rate, 18/min; and blood pressure, 102/65 mm Hg. He was well appearing with normal cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations. There was trace right lower extremity edema localized to the ankle and normal pedal pulses. Erythema without warmth was present over the right ankle and dorsomedial foot, along with nontender, nonpalpable purpura over the dorsum of the foot and scattered petechiae over the right lower leg (Figure). When the leg was elevated above the level of the heart, the surrounding erythema faded. Results of laboratory testing were as follows: white blood cell count, 6000/μL; hemoglobin level, 13.7 mg/dL; platelet count, 118 000/μL; creatinine level, 1.3 mg/dL (114.95 μmol/L); prothrombin time, 15.2 seconds (reference range, 12.2-14.9 seconds); activated partial thromboplastin time, 41 seconds (reference range, 23.1-34.2 seconds); C-reactive protein level, 7 mg/dL (reference range, 0-1 mg/dL); and normal urinalysis results.

options.B: Order antinuclear antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, and complement levels

distractors: Order skin biopsy

explanation: C. Order lower extremity duplex ultrasound The key to the correct diagnosis is the change in appearance of the rash with leg elevation. Localized, asymmetric, nonpalpable purpura in dependent areas is suggestive of a congestive vascular process. Recent trauma and reduced mobility are well recognized risk factors for thrombosis. Skin biopsy (choice A), as well as measurement of antinuclear antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, and complement levels (choice B), are appropriate tests for vasculitides that typically present as palpable purpura that is not positional or dependent, resulting from inflammation of small and medium vessels, often involving the lower extremities bilaterally. The absence of warmth, tenderness, and leukocytosis makes cellulitis less likely and antibiotic treatment (choice D) not appropriate. Fever and elevated C-reactive protein level are nonspecific findings and may be seen in any of the above scenarios; thus, recognizing atypical features of the rash helps avert clinicians from an extensive vasculitis evaluation or unnecessary antibiotic treatment. Doppler compression ultrasonography in this patient revealed an acute deep venous thrombosis (DVT) isolated to the posterior tibial vein. Purpura is a dermatologic manifestation of localized red blood cell extravasation, typically due to vascular congestion, vessel damage, or coagulopathy. The initial approach to patients with purpura should focus on general features, such as fever or toxic appearance, which may suggest life-threatening causes (eg, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, purpura fulminans, and other infectious exanthems).1Furthermore, purpura should be categorized as palpable or nonpalpable, with the former due to vessel inflammation, a hallmark of systemic vasculitides.2Of the nonpalpable purpuras, concomitant thrombocytopenia often suggests disorders of consumption (eg, immune thrombocytopenias or disseminated intravascular coagulation) or production (eg, bone marrow disorders), while normal platelet counts suggest a functional platelet disorder, vessel wall fragility, or impaired flow from obstruction. This patient’s mild thrombocytopenia, along with mildly prolonged prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time on presentation, were postulated to be consumptive because of acute thrombus formation and normalized on repeat testing. Features of the purpura described in this case, particularly dependency and localized distribution in a nontoxic patient, suggest vascular congestion of the plantar foot veins, which drain into the posterior tibial vein; the plantar veins were subsequently confirmed on ultrasound to be dilated and acutely thrombosed at the mid-calf level. It is unknown why DVT uncommonly presents with purpura as the dominant clinical finding. Currently, uncertainty exists regarding the optimal management strategy for isolated distal DVT. Two recent meta-analyses suggest benefit to anticoagulation vs no anticoagulation without an increase in risk of major bleeding.3,4Current guidelines propose assessment of symptoms and risk factors for thrombus extension (eg, extensive thrombus burden, active malignancy, history of venous thromboembolism [VTE], absence of a reversible provoking factor). In the absence of symptoms or risk factors, or if bleeding risk is high, holding anticoagulation and performing serial imaging to assess for thrombus extension is reasonable. In symptomatic patients and those with risk factors, an anticoagulation plan similar to that for the management of proximal venous thromboembolism is recommended.5,6 Thrombophilia testing is not required for cases of DVT for which there is a known provoking risk factor. Testing may be considered in affected patients who are young with unprovoked VTE and have a strong family history of VTE, patients with recurrent VTE, or female family members considering pregnancy or use of oral contraceptives.7 The patient started rivaroxaban and was discharged. After 1 week, the petechiae and purpura significantly improved, followed by complete resolution approximately 1 month later. He completed a 4-month course of anticoagulation.

scenario: A 32-year-old Nigerian woman presented with dull pain, pruritus, and discoloration of the dorsal aspect of both feet for 18 months. Her medical history included a red blood cell transfusion as a child and 2 uncomplicated pregnancies. The lesions started as small papules on the dorsal right great toe and left third toe that gradually spread across the dorsum of her feet over the following 12 months. An over-the-counter antifungal ointment was unhelpful. Her primary care physician completed a biopsy, diagnosed verruca plantaris, and prescribed topical salicylic acid twice daily for 4 weeks. The lesions did not improve, and her foot pain worsened. Subsequent treatment with topical liquid nitrogen cryotherapy was ineffective. Three months after cryotherapy, the patient presented to the dermatology clinic regarding the lesions on her feet. The patient stated that the lesions had been stable in size for the previous 6 months, without bleeding, discharge, or change in color. She continued to have 6 of 10, dull, constant pain that was nonradiating, improved when she soaked her feet in water, and worsened with any type of topical pressure or wrapping. Physical examination revealed multiple well-circumscribed, scaly plaques with cobblestone surfaces on the dorsal aspects of the forefoot and midfoot bilaterally. Findings were more severe on the right and left hindfoot (Figure, left panel). On serologic testing, the patient was negative for HIV and positive for hepatitis C virus (HCV). A punch biopsy of the right foot lesion revealed psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia, parakeratosis, eosinophils, papillary dermal inflammation, and intraepidermal necrosis (Figure, right panel).
