explanation: Hepatitis C–induced necrolytic acral erythema (NAE) D. Prescribe oral zinc therapy The keys to the correct diagnosis in this case were the childhood history of a red blood cell transfusion associated with acquisition of HCV, the dorsal distribution of lesions, and intraepidermal necrosis on the biopsy.1,2In patients with hepatitis C–induced NAE, the combination of hypertrophic verrucous plaques and microscopic findings of psoriasiform hyperplasia commonly result in the misdiagnosis of psoriasis, eczematous dermatitis, or hypertrophic lichen planus.3Because the punch biopsy provided diagnostic information, an incisional biopsy (choice A) was not required. Additionally, the case offers no clinical indications for the use of antibiotics (choice B) or further imaging (choice C). Hepatitis C affects approximately 71.1 million people worldwide.4Hepatitis C–induced NAE was first described in Egypt in 1996,3first identified in the US in 2000,2and currently has a prevalence of 1.7% in patients with chronic HCV infection.5Initially, NAE was considered a pathognomonic marker for hepatitis C; however, recent cases have been reported in seronegative patients with hepatitis C.3,6The etiology of hepatitis C–induced NAE is likely multifactorial.7The principal theory regarding the pathogenesis of NAE is that chronic HCV infection causes hepatocellular dysfunction, resulting in hypoalbuminemia, abnormal zinc metabolism, and decreased epidermal zinc levels, leading to keratinocyte necrolysis.5,7Hepatitis C–induced NAE typically presents with well-defined superficial hyperpigmented pruritic and necrotic vesiculobullous lesions that later coalesce into velvety hyperkeratotic plaques with a rim of dusky erythema.2The distribution of lesions and subsequent plaques is on the acral surfaces of the body, including the dorsum of the feet, Achilles tendons, lower and upper leg, and dorsal surfaces of the hands. The periorificial and oral mucosa usually are not affected.1-3In a study of 30 Egyptian patients with hepatitis C–induced NAE, all patients had cutaneous manifestations on the feet. Sites most commonly affected were the toes (97%), lateral malleolus (90%), and ankles (83%).1 There is no definitive treatment for hepatitis C–induced NAE. In 9 patients, mild improvement of lesions was reported using topical steroids with and without UV-B phototherapy and hyperalimentation with zinc and protein supplementation.1,5,8Complete resolution of lesions and symptoms were reported with topical tacrolimus, UV-B phototherapy, and oral zinc monotherapy.1,5Case reports have suggested therapeutic benefit from zinc in the treatment of hepatitis C–induced NAE, but no randomized trials have been completed and therefore benefits of zinc remain unclear.2,3,7,8Zinc has anti-inflammatory, immunostimulatory, antioxidant, and antiviral properties.7In one study, patients with NAE had significantly lower serum zinc levels and a lower abundance of zinc in skin lesions compared with healthy controls.9Treating the underlying HCV infection was associated with improvement in the cutaneous lesions, as demonstrated in case reports with patients treated with interferon with and without zinc supplementation, ribavirin, and liver transplantation.1-3,5,7Although limited data exist on the use of new oral direct-acting antivirals in patients with hepatitis C–related cutaneous manifestations, 8 investigational studies and 5 case reports have demonstrated the effectiveness of oral direct-acting antivirals in patients with HCV-associated mixed cryoglobulinemia in achieving a sustained virologic response, clinical response, and improvement of symptoms.10 Recognition of hepatitis C–induced NAE may facilitate early diagnosis and treatment of HCV.1,2In one study, hepatitis C–induced NAE was the presenting symptom in 26 of 30 patients (87%) unaware of their underlying HCV infection.1 The patient was treated with oral zinc monotherapy twice daily. After 3 months of therapy, the lesions had substantially improved (eFigure in theSupplement). Subsequently, the patient discontinued therapy because of overwhelming medication-related nausea. In follow-up clinic appointments, the patient’s lesions were unchanged since zinc was discontinued, without any new lesions, and she continued to be without pain. Initially, the patient declined treated of her underlying hepatitis C because of the cost. However, the patient recently was able to acquire health insurance and plans to begin therapy.

scenario: A 64-year-old man presented with concern about an abnormal genetic test result for apolipoprotein E (APOE) obtained through his primary care physician. He reported forgetfulness and word-finding difficulties for 3 years but performed all activities of daily living independently and was generally healthy. His father and maternal great aunt developed dementia in their 70s. Physical (including neurologic) examination, basic laboratory studies, and brain magnetic resonance imaging results were normal. The Short Test of Mental Status (STMS) score was 33 (maximal attainable score of 38 indicates best performance). Neuropsychological assessment showed average to above-average performance in all cognitive domains, accounting for age and education. Results of his genetic testing forAPOEwere reported as follows: “This individual possesses an apolipoprotein E genotype (3 and 4) that indicates, with high specificity, that Alzheimer’s disease is the cause of or a contributor to the observed dementia.”

explanation: C. Reassure and address patient’s concerns and follow up in 1 year. Most cases of Alzheimer disease are sporadic and are thought to be influenced by multiple heritable and nonheritable factors. TheAPOEgene (19q32.13) codes for apolipoprotein E and has 3 common isoforms (ɛ2, ɛ3, and ɛ4) defined by specific base-pair variations (ie, single-nucleotide variations [SNVs]).APOE ɛ3is the most commonallele(worldwide prevalence, 78%) and has no association with Alzheimer disease risk.1WhileAPOE ɛ2(worldwide prevalence, 8%) is associated with a lower rate of Alzheimer disease (odds ratio [OR], 0.6 vs ɛ3/ɛ3),APOE ɛ4(14%) is the strongest known genetic susceptibility factor for sporadic Alzheimer disease (OR, 8-12 for ɛ4/ɛ4 vs ɛ3/ɛ3;Table)2,3and is associated with reduced age of Alzheimer disease onset by approximately 2.5 years per allele copy.4The main function of apolipoprotein E is mediating extracellular lipid transport and cellular lipid uptake, the latter through a process known as endocytosis. Although its precise role in Alzheimer disease pathophysiology is unclear, proposed mechanisms forAPOE ɛ4include promoting amyloid deposition, impairing amyloid clearance via modulating the activity of macrophages known as microglia, and influencing synaptic plasticity, defined as the ability to change the strength of connections between neurons.1 APOE ɛ4is neither necessary nor sufficient for the development of Alzheimer disease dementia, and meta-analyses indicate low sensitivity (53%) and specificity (67%) ofAPOE ɛ4for identifying patients who will progress from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer disease dementia.2Given this background and the lack of disease-modifying therapies for Alzheimer disease, evidence does not support obtainingAPOEgenotyping in the clinical evaluation of patients with cognitive symptoms or impairment. However,APOEallele testing is available for patients who wish to pay out of pocket (approximately $138) and is commonly completed by direct-to-consumer genetic screening services, which perform targeted tests for base-pairvariantsfrom DNA typically obtained from saliva, cheek swab, or blood specimens. Medicare does not currently coverAPOE ɛ4testing. The patient presented with concern about impending cognitive decline based on genetic screening results. The patient’s STMS score, equivalent to a Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score of 27 (score range, 0 [worst] to 30 [best]), was in a range that could be seen with normal cognition or early mild cognitive impairment.5Detailed neuropsychological testing is not recommended on the basis ofAPOEallele status, but may be considered for obtaining more information about the presence, character, and extent of cognitive impairment when these measures are not adequately ascertained by clinical examination. Although the genetic test result for this patient included language to suggest that Alzheimer disease was a cause of or contributor to the patient's cognitive symptoms, the unremarkable neuropsychological testing (within expected range based on age and education), neurologic examination, and brain magnetic resonance imaging do not support a diagnosis of dementia or Alzheimer disease. The presence of a single first-degree relative with Alzheimer disease dementia is associated with increased risk (relative risk, 1.73) that is weaker than the risk conferred byAPOE ɛ4.6Additional diagnostic testing is not warranted, andAPOE ɛ4 status would not change clinical care. The neuropathological features of Alzheimer disease include amyloid plaques and hyperphosphorylated tau in the brain parenchyma. CSF biomarkers (low CSF amyloid and high CSF phosphorylated tau) can identify Alzheimer disease pathophysiologic changes in the central nervous system, but negative results from this invasive test do not rule out Alzheimer disease dementia in the future. Although not directly indicative of amyloid and tau pathology, FDG-PET can differentiate Alzheimer disease from frontotemporal dementia based on its distinctive pattern of decreased temporoparietal glucose uptake, which can precede visualized atrophy in these regions on magnetic resonance imaging. FDG-PET was unnecessary for this patient because of the lack of clinical features of either cause of dementia. Patient education onAPOE ɛ4can be accomplished in a primary care setting or in a neurology clinic and does not necessarily require formal genetic counseling. Amyloid PET imaging consists of noninvasive detection of elevated amyloid in the brain and may be useful in patients with cognitive impairment of uncertain etiology and when a molecular diagnosis of Alzheimer disease would alter management.7However, greater than 70% of individuals older than age 65 who have a positive amyloid PET scan and normal cognition never develop dementia in their lifetime,8limiting the utility of amyloid PET in people with normal cognitive function. Blood-based assays for amyloid and tau have shown promise in the research setting.9 The patient was counseled on the relationship betweenAPOE ɛ4and Alzheimer disease and provided with information about lifestyle interventions to help maintain cognition (via cognitive and social engagement, physical exercise, healthy diet, quality sleep, and control of cerebrovascular disease risk factors), and scheduled for follow-up.10Two years following the identification of the positiveAPOE ɛ4test result, the patient continues to have subjective memory and word-finding concerns but has not demonstrated cognitive decline on repeat neuropsychological testing.

scenario: A 19-month-old boy presented for evaluation of widespread edema and acute dermatitis. Following an upper respiratory tract infection 1 month prior, he developed disseminated red, scaly patches and a progressive eruption of hyperpigmented and hypopigmented patches of skin. He had occasional nonbloody loose stools but no fevers or vomiting. Although he was otherwise well, his growth had fallen from the 75th to the 25th percentile for height and weight over the preceding 9 months, and he could speak only 2 words. His medical history was notable for atopic dermatitis and diarrhea in infancy that prompted allergy testing at age 6 months; he was subsequently diagnosed with milk, egg, and peanut allergies. His parents avoided feeding him these foods, providing him only soy-based milk and formula, with improvement of dermatitis, until age 1 year. Since then his diet had consisted of multiple rice milk feeds daily, supplemented only with pureed fruits and vegetables, pasta, snack puffs, and sunflower butter. The patient had no history of meconium ileus or family history of cystic fibrosis. There was no recent travel and no changes to the home environment. On presentation, the patient was irritable, with normal vital signs. He displayed prominent scrotal swelling and pitting edema of the legs bilaterally. Skin examination was notable for erythematous, denuded patches with peeling scale and reticulate hyperpigmentation, accentuated on the abdomen, back, diaper area, and extensor extremities (Figure; left panel). Notably, his skin also demonstrated widespread patches of hypopigmentation, with an accompanying band of hypopigmentation proximally at the site of newest hair growth (Figure; right panel).

options.A: Check levels of serum protein, albumin, prealbumin, and other nutritional laboratory measures
options.B: Check urinalysis and urine microscopy to evaluate for protein in urine

answer: Check levels of protein, albumin, prealbumin, and other nutritional laboratory measures
distractors: Check urinalysis and urine microscopy to evaluate for protein in urine
Perform a skin biopsy
Treat with topical steroids
explanation: A. Check levels of protein, albumin, prealbumin, and other nutritional laboratory measures The key to the correct diagnosis in this case is recognizing edema, exfoliative dermatitis, and pigmentary dilution in an irritable child who consumes a relatively protein-deficient diet. This can be confirmed via laboratory evaluation revealing low levels of prealbumin, albumin, and total protein, as identified in this patient (prealbumin, 11 mg/dL; albumin, 1.7 g/dL; total protein, 3.8 g/dL) (choice A). Obtaining a urinalysis (choice B) is incorrect, as the edema of kwashiorkor is not secondary to protein loss in urine. The histologic features of kwashiorkor are not unique, and biopsy is not required for diagnosis (choice C).1-3Kwashiorkor may be mistaken for atopic dermatitis or precipitated by well-intentioned parents who restrict their child’s nutrition in an effort to treat the condition.4While topical steroids (choice D) may improve the dermatitis of kwashiorkor, this would not address the underlying cause. Kwashiorkor is the edematous form of protein-energy malnutrition; it typically affects infants and children at the age of weaning from breast milk or formula through 5 years.1,5Clinically, kwashiorkor is characterized by a distinct “peeling paint” dermatitis with diffuse erythema, desquamation, and hyperpigmentation, accompanied by widespread loss of skin pigmentation.1,4,6Alternating light and dark bands may be appreciated in sparse or brittle hair of afflicted individuals.1,5Importantly, extensive edema may increase weight gain and obscure associated growth failure, delaying diagnosis.1 Kwashiorkor occurs worldwide, across socioeconomic strata.6In developed countries, nutritional ignorance (exacerbated by barriers to accessing health care, financial stress, and social chaos), fad diets, and avoidance of food groups secondary to presumed allergy may precipitate kwashiorkor, particularly if low-protein milk alternatives (eg, rice milk, nondairy creamer, excessively diluted formula) are provided as primary sources of nutrition, as for this patient.1,6A complete dietary history (including access to and affordability of food) is critical to making the proper diagnosis. Clinicians should inquire about the type, frequency, and amount of foods an individual consumes, methods of formula preparation, and consumption of and allergies to protein-rich foods. The differential diagnosis of kwashiorkor includes malabsorptive syndromes, such as cystic fibrosis.7Other nutritional deficiencies, including acrodermatitis enteropathica secondary to zinc deficiency, should also be considered.1These 2 eczematous dermatoses share overlapping features and often present concomitantly but can be differentiated by their distribution—acrodermatitis enteropathica preferentially involves perioral, anogenital, and periungual sites, while involvement in kwashiorkor is more diffuse.1,8Measurement of serum zinc levels and sweat chloride testing should therefore be performed in children evaluated for kwashiorkor.1,8Measurement of immunoglobulin levels and HIV serologic testing may be indicated to rule out primary or acquired immunodeficiency in children with exfoliative dermatitis and frequent infections, unusual infections, or both, while levels of serum amino acids, urine organic acids, or both may identify metabolic disorders in patients with failure to thrive accompanied by developmental delay, lethargy, or progressive neurologic deterioration. The widespread edema of kwashiorkor may mimic nephrotic syndrome, but its causes in children (ie, minimal-change disease) do not have distinct cutaneous findings.9 Treating kwashiorkor requires special attention to monitoring and managing temperature, hypoglycemia, dehydration, micronutrient deficiencies, and occult infection.2Importantly, nutrient repletion should be initiated with small, frequent, enteric feeds, and electrolytes should be closely monitored and corrected to avoid refeeding syndrome.2,3Refeeding syndrome consists of electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, hypomagnesemia) that may precipitate cardiac arrhythmias, respiratory failure, and death.10Application of emollients and low-potency topical steroids can mitigate the dermatitis of kwashiorkor. The patient was admitted and treated with frequent, small, nasogastric feeds of peptide-based formula and skin-directed emollient therapy. As the volume of his feeds gradually increased, he experienced clinically asymptomatic hypophosphatemia requiring supplementation. After 9 days, his dermatitis and edema had improved, and he was discharged with nutritional support. He gradually transitioned to protein-rich solid foods. Although he still has productive speech delay at nearly 4 years of age, his growth and development have otherwise normalized and his nutrition-associated kwashiorkor has not recurred.
